content: Output safety / fallback cleanup bug: if `originalPath == outPath`, `File.Copy` throws ("source and destination must not be the same") and the catch then calls `File.Delete(outPath)` — which deletes the user's source document. Separately, when `ReviseInPlace` throws, the partially-edited `outPath` is left in place and `WordprocessingDocument.Create` refuses to overwrite existing files, so the documented "guaranteed fallback" silently fails. Guard against `PathsEqual(originalPath, outPath)` and delete the partial output in the second catch as well.

Leading-insertion position bug: the comment claims a null anchor inserts at the body start, but `body.InsertBefore(para, sect)` puts the paragraph immediately before the section properties — which is the LAST direct child of the body, not the first. `body.Append` likewise appends to the end. New leading content silently lands at the document tail. Insert before the first body child instead.

Non-text run fidelity loss: `UnwrapHyperlinks` permanently removes `w:hyperlink` wrappers so rejecting a revision cannot restore hyperlink targets (only the rPr/Hyperlink style remains). `MarkParagraphDeleted` / `ReviseParagraph` also rebuild runs containing any text using `RunWithText`, which drops `w:sym`, `w:drawing`, `w:footnoteReference`, `w:noBreakHyphen` (mapped to plain `-`), `w:tab`/`w:posTab` distinctions, field-code runs (`w:instrText` / `w:fldChar`), and SDT/customXml content. `InnerRuns` likewise ignores existing `w:ins` / `w:del` wrappers, so the diff is computed against an "accepted" view of the source. Consider preserving hyperlink wrappers around the inserted/deleted runs (they are legal inside `w:ins`/`w:del`) and emitting untouched run children verbatim instead of reconstructing them from `RunText`.

Table-row revisions are not structural: a row "deletion" only wraps the text of each cell paragraph in `w:del` — the row itself is never marked via `<w:trPr><w:del .../>`, so accepting the revision leaves a visibly-empty row in the table. Conversely, row-count changes are emitted by `InsertRevisedParagraph` as ordinary body paragraphs (not new `w:tr` rows with cell paragraphs), and the cell-count mismatch fallback deletes the row and inserts a plain paragraph — destroying the table structure entirely. Use `w:trPr/w:del`/`w:ins` on the row for deletions, and construct real `w:tr` rows (with cells) when the diff asks for a new or replaced row.

Unbounded LCS allocation for paragraph-level diff: `DiffList` always materializes an `(n+1)*(m+1)` `int` matrix with no size cap, unlike `DiffText` which limits itself to 4M cells. With untrusted or large documents (paragraph counts in the tens of thousands), `int[n+1, m+1]` can exceed available memory and crash the process — also a denial-of-service surface if the CLI is fed arbitrary JSON. Apply the same `MaxCells` cap (or fall back to a coarse replace opcode) as `DiffText` does.

The global :focus-visible rule sets `border-radius: var(--r-sm)` on every element that gains keyboard focus. Because the property is applied to the element itself (not the outline), it mutates the element's actual border-radius — any element without an explicit radius will snap from 0 → 8px on focus and back on blur (visible jank on native <button>/<select>/<a>), and elements with custom radii (e.g., pill-shaped `.nm-tag` at 9999px) will be overridden while focus is visible. Remove the border-radius from this rule so the outline shape follows each element's own radius in modern browsers; if a uniform focus shape is desired, scope it to a specific selector rather than every focused element.

No error handling for missing vendor package: readdirSync(src) will throw an unhandled ENOENT when @lobehub/icons-static-svg is not installed (e.g., optional peer in CI, fresh clone without `npm install`, monorepo hoisting edge cases). Add an existence check (existsSync) and a friendly message, or wrap the whole script body in try/catch with a non-zero exit so CI fails loudly instead of with a raw stack trace.
existing_code:
const src = join(root, "node_modules/@lobehub/icons-static-svg/icons");
const dest = join(root, "src/assets/providers/lobe");

content: readFileSync and JSON.parse have no try/catch. Wrap the I/O + parse in try/catch and emit a clear localized error (e.g., `无法读取 <path>: <err.message>`) so contributors can diagnose without reading V8 internals.

Move the reads inside helper functions (or wrap in a fixture with a clear skip/fail message) so a missing file produces a per-test failure with actionable diagnostics instead of crashing `pytest --collect`.

content: All three regexes use `[A-Z_]+`, so any future code containing digits (e.g. `HTTP_404`, `INVALID_ARG_2`) or lowercase letters is silently dropped — `test_rust_enum_has_codes_and_no_duplicates` will still pass because `rust_codes()` only sees the partial set, and `test_frontend_union_matches_rust_enum` will then report a phantom "Rust 独有 / 前端独有" mismatch blaming the wrong side. This is a false negative on the cross-language gate; widen the character class (e.g. `[A-Z0-9_]+` or `r"[A-Z][A-Z0-9_]*"`) to match the actual wire-protocol naming policy.

content: `ts_codes()` re-runs `re.findall(r'"([A-Z_]+)"', body)` over the raw slice between `export type CommandErrorCode =` and the next `;`, so a JSDoc or `// ...` comment inside that slice (e.g. `// legacy alias "FOO_BAR"`) is silently captured as a real code, polluting both the set comparison and the order assertion with no diagnostic hint that the extra string came from a comment. Strip `//` and `/* */` from the slice (or tokenize the TS body) before extracting literals.
suggestion_code:
body = ERROR_HANDLER_TS[start:end]
    body = re.sub(r"//[^\n]*", "", body)            # strip line comments
    body = re.sub(r"/\*.*?\*/", "", body, flags=re.S)  # strip block comments
    return re.findall(r'"([A-Z][A-Z0-9_]*)"', body)

content: `registered_plugins` only matches `tauri_plugin_xxx::init`. Modern tauri plugins are commonly registered with `tauri_plugin_xxx::Builder::new()...build()` (e.g. `tauri_plugin_log::Builder::new().build()`); those `.plugin(...)` calls will be silently dropped from the registered set, and `test_plugin_calls_have_registered_plugin` will then falsely fail with "plugin not registered" on a correct codebase. Either generalise the regex (e.g. accept `tauri_plugin_(\w+)::(?:init|Builder)`) or also scan inside `.plugin(...)` argument lists.

The closure emit regex `(?<![\w.])emit\("..."` has no awareness of comments, doc-comments (`/// calls emit("foo") …`) or raw string literals (e.g. `r"emit("foo")"`). All of those populate `backend` with events that are never actually emitted at runtime, so `test_listened_events_have_emitter` will pass even when a real `emit(...)` has been removed/commented out, masking listener-without-emitter bugs. Consider stripping Rust line/doc comments and raw strings before scanning, or restricting matches to inside `fn`/`let emit =` blocks.

`frontend_invokes` only matches a hard-coded double-quoted literal with at most one generic level: `<[^>]*>` rejects nested generics such as `invoke<Promise<MyType>>("foo")`; template literals (`invoke(\`cmd_${id}\`)`), single quotes, and indirect dispatch (`const c = "foo"; invoke(c)`) are all skipped. The whole point of this audit is to catch "frontend calls an unregistered command" at lint time, so silently dropping these patterns means real production invokes against unregistered commands become false negatives. Either broaden the regex to accept single quotes and template literals, or add a fallback AST-based scan.

Raw strings `r#"..."#` (and `r##"..."##`, `br#"..."#`) are not recognized. The handler enters string mode at the first `"` and exits at the next, so embedded `"` characters leak source text into the cleaned output. Example: `r#"x "thread_rng" y"#` becomes `r#` + stripped `"x "` + `thread_rng` + stripped `" y"` + `#`, leaving `thread_rng` in the cleaned text — this would produce a false positive for an audit gate whose entire purpose is to flag exactly this token. Same hazard for false negatives on `evolution::strategy` if a data-layer file wrapped a strategy reference inside a raw string to bypass the linter.
suggestion_code:
elif c == '"':
            # 识别 r"/br"/r#"/br# 等原始字符串前缀（含任意数量 #）。
            # 原字符进入字符串模式后，必须等到匹配的 "#...#" 才退出，
            # 否则嵌入的 " 会让后续源码泄漏到 cleaned 文本里。
            prefix_start = i
            j = i - 1
            while j >= 0 and text[j] in ('r', 'b'):
                j -= 1
            raw_prefix = text[j + 1:i]
            hash_count = 0
            if raw_prefix and all(c in ('r', 'b') for c in raw_prefix) and 'r' in raw_prefix:
                while i < n and text[i] == '#':
                    hash_count += 1
                    i += 1
                closer = '"' + '#' * hash_count
                end = text.find(closer, i)
                if end == -1:
                    i = n
                else:
                    i = end + len(closer)
                out.append("\n" if text[i - 1:i] == "\n" else " ")
                continue
            in_string = True
            out.append(" ")

content: `strip_cfg_test_modules` only matches the exact attribute `#[cfg(test)]`. Real test modules frequently use `#[cfg(all(test, feature = "..."))]`, `#[cfg(any(test, debug_assertions))]`, or stack `#[cfg(test)]` after other attributes separated by other items, so legitimate test-only usages of forbidden identifiers will surface as false positives and either get suppressed by developers (who learn the audit is noisy) or block legitimate code. Either broaden the pattern to `cfg\s*\(\s*(?:any|all)?\([^)]*\btest\b[^)]*\)` or document the limitation explicitly and exempt known combined-cfg test modules.
suggestion_code:
# 兼容 #[cfg(test)] / #[cfg(all(test, ...))] / #[cfg(any(test, ...))]
    pattern = re.compile(
        r"#\[cfg\s*\(\s*(?:all|any)?\s*\([^)]*\btest\b[^)]*\)\s*\]\s*"
        r"[^{}]*?mod\s+\w+\s*\{"
    )
existing_code: pattern = re.compile(r"#\[cfg\(test\)\][^{}]*?mod\s+\w+\s*\{")

content: strip_comments_and_strings treats everything between backticks as opaque string content and replaces it with spaces, including `${...}` interpolation expressions. Code like `` `result: ${eval(input)}` `` has the `eval(input)` body erased to whitespace, so EVAL_RE never matches it. Template-literal interpolation is very common in modern TS/TSX (dynamic class names, tagged-template helpers, error-format helpers, inline i18n), so this is a realistic false-negative path the audit does not catch. The header enumerates the regex-literal limitation but not this one — only WebView runtime CSP stands between an audit miss and a blocked execution. Consider tracking `${...}` nesting with a small stack inside the backtick branch and re-entering normal scanning for the expression body until the matching `}` closes it.

INDIRECT_RE enumerates only `(0,eval)`, `window.eval`, `globalThis.eval`, `self.eval`, and there is no eval-side equivalent of ALIAS_RE (which exists only for `Function`). Real obfuscation routes that slip past the audit:
1. `var e = eval; e('x')` — aliasing; `eval;` does not match EVAL_RE (needs `(`), and `e(` matches nothing.
2. `globalThis['eval']('x')` / `window["eval"]('x')` — computed access; the `'eval'`/`"eval"` literal is stripped to whitespace by the stripper, leaving `globalThis[  ]('x')` with no `eval` token at all, so neither EVAL_RE nor INDIRECT_RE fires.
3. `eval?.('x')` — optional chaining; `\beval\s*\(` requires `(` directly after `eval` and `\s*` does not match `?.`.
4. `Reflect.apply(eval, this, ['x'])` / `Function.prototype.constructor.call(...)` — reflective invocation.
Each of these is a reachable way to execute `eval`, so the indirect-form detector under-covers relative to its stated goal. Consider adding patterns for `\b\w+\s*=\s*eval\b` (alias), `(?:\bwindow\b|\bglobalThis\b|\bself\b|\bglobal\b)\s*\[\s*['"`]eval['"`]\s*\]` (computed), `\beval\s*\?\s*\(`, and `Reflect\s*\.\s*(?:apply|construct)\s*\([^,]*\beval\b`.
suggestion_code:
EVAL_ALIAS_RE = r"\b\w+\s*=\s*" + EVAL + r"\b"
EVAL_COMPUTED_RE = (
    r"(?:\bwindow\b|\bglobalThis\b|\bself\b|\bglobal\b)"
    r"\s*\[\s*['\"`]" + EVAL + r"['\"`]\s*\]"
)
EVAL_OPTCHAIN_RE = r"\b" + EVAL + r"\s*\?\s*\("
EVAL_REFLECT_RE = (
    r"\bReflect\s*\.\s*(?:apply|construct)\s*\([^,]*\b" + EVAL + r"\b"
)
INDIRECT_RE = (
    r"\(0,\s*" + EVAL + r"\)"
    r"|window\." + EVAL + r"\b"
    r"|globalThis\." + EVAL + r"\b"
    r"|self\." + EVAL + r"\b"
    r"|" + EVAL_ALIAS_RE
    r"|" + EVAL_COMPUTED_RE
    r"|" + EVAL_OPTCHAIN_RE
    r"|" + EVAL_REFLECT_RE
)
existing_code:
INDIRECT_RE = (
    r"\(0,\s*" + EVAL + r"\)"
    r"|window\." + EVAL + r"\b"
    r"|globalThis\." + EVAL + r"\b"
    r"|self\." + EVAL + r"\b"
)

content: Body is converted via `String::from_utf8_lossy(&buf).into_owned()`, which silently replaces invalid UTF-8 bytes with U+FFFD. For what is almost certainly a JSON/UTF-8 API, this masks malformed bodies (which should surface as `Malformed` → 400), lets a sender alter parsed semantics via replacement characters, and breaks content-length-sensitive checks downstream that compared against raw bytes. Use `String::from_utf8(buf)` and map the error to `BodyRead::Malformed` (or extend the enum with a `NotUtf8` variant → 400).
existing_code: BodyRead::Ok(String::from_utf8_lossy(&buf).into_owned())

content: `SabotageStore::upsert` simulates concurrency by mutating `updated_at` inside the *same* thread, before delegating to `MemStore::upsert`, and relies on MemStore's specific lock-acquisition order to trigger the 409 path. The inline comment flags the fragility, but the actual risk is silent false-positive: if `MemStore::upsert` ever wraps the whole operation in a single lock (or changes the compare order), the test still asserts 409 even though the conflict path is no longer being exercised — masking regressions in the most important write-safety guarantee. Replace the sequential trick with a real concurrent writer (a separate thread that bumps `updated_at` while the handler is sleeping in `MemStore::load`), or at minimum inject the mutation through a hook that MemStore exposes for tests.

Mutex held across blocking joins in `api_stop_locked`. The `state.0` guard passed in as `&mut Option<RunningApi>` is held by the caller (`api_stop_impl` / `rotate_apply`) for the entire duration of this call. The body blocks on `h.join()` (accept thread — comment cites ~400ms worst case) and then `stop_sse_writers(...)` (comment cites `SSE_STOP_JOIN_TIMEOUT` = 5s). Any concurrent `api_start` / `api_status` / `api_rotate_token` trying to take `state.0` is serialized behind this for up to ~5.4s, directly contradicting the file-level invariant that the lock only covers short in-memory mutations. Restructure to set the shutdown flag and grab the join handles under the lock, then drop the guard before doing the joins.

File I/O and port bind performed under `state.0` mutex in `api_rotate_token` Err recovery. The inner `Ok(mut g) => { ... }` block holds the mutex guard across two `std::fs::read_to_string(&path)` calls AND `api_start_locked(...)` (which binds `API_PORT` and spawns threads). This directly violates the module's documented convention "文件 I/O 一律在锁释放后做" and re-introduces the very serialization the design was meant to avoid. Drop the guard, do the file I/O and start_api outside the lock, then re-acquire to merge the new `RunningApi` into the Option — accepting the small TOCTOU window, since the alternative is blocking all API commands on filesystem + bind latency.

TOCTOU window between `service_present` re-check and `write_enabled_flag` in `api_start`. The comment itself admits "复核≠原子". Between `service_present(&state) != Some(false)` and `write_enabled_flag(&app)`, a concurrent `api_stop` (or a second `api_start` that took a fresh instance) can flip `state.0` such that the flag ends up describing the opposite of the in-memory truth. The comment says this is self-healing on next manual toggle, but a single race flips the persisted state for every subsequent boot until the user notices. Either (a) drop the re-check and accept the worst-case, or (b) make the in-memory state itself authoritative (e.g. record the decision in `ApiState` under the same lock as the `Option` mutation, and write the flag in a single follow-up that re-reads with no intervening command surface — not achievable with the current two-phase design).

Symmetric TOCTOU in `api_status` between `service_present` re-check and `clear_enabled_flag`. Same defect as `api_start`: between the re-check and the flag clear, a concurrent `api_start` may have already bound the port and written its own flag, in which case this clear silently undoes the user's just-issued start, persisting as "disabled" until the next manual toggle. The inline comment acknowledges "误清后果可由用户手动开关自愈" — that's documenting a known correctness bug, not solving it.

tmp 清理失败被 `let _` 静默吞掉：rename 或 write_all 失败后 `remove_file(&tmp)` 不上报，tmp 中存的是**明文 token**。清理失败（磁盘满/AV 锁/进程被杀留下半截文件/只读 FS）意味着把密钥直接泄到磁盘且调用方零感知。安全后果与"flag 失败只 eprintln"完全不在一个等级。建议至少 eprintln 清理失败，或把未清理的 tmp 路径记到一个待清理列表里（下次启动扫描回收）。

`tighten_token_permissions` 在读取路径上用 `let _` 静默吞掉 chmod 失败：legacy 0644 文件若因 immutable 位 / 只读 FS / NFS 属性不可 chmod，token 永久以 world-readable 残留，调用方零感知。注释里"best-effort，失败不挡读"把一次性的安全修复变成了静默安全降级——这恰恰是最敏感的文件。建议至少把 chmod 失败 eprintln（或返回 Result 由 caller 决策），与 tmp 清理失败同等对待。

Commit/SSE consistency gap: `notify_change` is a separate default method, not part of `upsert`. The documented real-time guarantee depends on every caller remembering to invoke it after a successful commit. An omitted call leaves SSE clients permanently stale; a call made before commit (or after a failed one) announces uncommitted state. Enforce post-commit notification inside the store (e.g., invoke it at the end of `upsert` on success) or return the broadcast result so callers can't accidentally skip it.

Sync-to-async bridge safety: `load`/`upsert` use `tauri::async_runtime::block_on`, guarded only by a thread-local Tokio-handle check that panics on violation. This is a fragile cross-layer contract that will bring down a request worker (and potentially the whole app if panic=abort) if any future caller runs on a Tokio task, in an async command handler, or from a Tauri callback. Either model the trait as async, or isolate the bridge behind a dedicated blocking pool and return an error instead of panicking when the invariant is violated.

History-lock poisoning is silently swallowed (`if let Ok(...)`) inside `broadcast()`. If `history` is ever poisoned, the event is broadcast live, persisted to disk (`next_id` is committed), and clients receive it — but it never enters the replay buffer. A reconnecting client with `Last-Event-ID` = (this id - 1) will skip this event forever, silently desyncing from the live stream. The file's own contract (`id 契约`) requires history to be authoritative for dedup; this branch violates it without any log or recovery. Either abort the broadcast with `return` (and roll the id back, like the atomic_write failure path), or explicitly log + record in a parallel journal.

The `clients` lock poison recovery uses `e.into_inner()`, which returns the inner `MutexGuard` — bypassing the poison flag but NOT validating that the guarded `Vec<(SyncSender, Weak)>` is in a logically consistent state. If a previous holder panicked mid-mutation (e.g., between `try_send` and `clients.remove(i)`), the vec may contain stale senders that have already been observed-failed by some other path, or partial updates. Subsequent broadcasts would push to / remove entries in a vec whose invariants are unverified. Either fail closed (`return` with diagnostic, mirroring the atomic_write failure path) or document why the vec's mutation pattern is panic-safe.

`write_event` reached from a `#[tauri::command]` violates the BOT_LOG_LOCK contract: the doc on `BOT_LOG_LOCK` says "持锁跨越整段阻塞文件 IO（rotate + open + chmod + write），不得在 tokio worker / 延迟敏感路径上直接调用", yet this command dispatches on Tauri's async runtime and synchronously runs `rotate_log_if_large` + `open` + `chmod` + `writeln` while holding the global mutex, blocking the worker. Either move the synchronous work into a `std::thread::spawn` (or `tauri::async_runtime::spawn_blocking`) before invoking `write_event`, or split write_event into a lock-free append path guarded by `spawn_blocking`. Same hazard applies to any caller of `audit_event!` / `write_event_with_error` from a `#[tauri::command]` or async task.

CONFIG_WRITE_LOCK is held across blocking keyring I/O. `migrate_legacy_key` calls `keyring::has_api_key()` and `keyring::write_api_key(&k)` while the lock is held (same pattern in `strip_verified_keys` / `migrate_search_keys` / `migrate_mcp_server_secrets_locked`). The header comment claims the lock only guards RMW file writes, but in practice lock duration scales with keyring backend latency (e.g. macOS Keychain prompts, Windows Credential Manager, libsecret dbus round-trips). This serializes every config write behind the slowest path and risks re-entrancy if any keyring call ever fires the audit logger from a callback. Either do keyring IO before acquiring the lock (commit in-memory only, then re-verify under lock), or split into per-resource locks.

`write_memory_tuning_at` takes its own `TUNING_WRITE_LOCK` that is independent of `CONFIG_WRITE_LOCK`, so it is not synchronized with `update_config_file` / `add_allowed_dir` / `migrate_*` (which write the same file under `CONFIG_WRITE_LOCK`). Two concurrent writers — e.g. one RMW-updating `evolution` and one RMW-updating `memoryTuning` — both read the same JSON snapshot, then the last writer silently overwrites the other's unrelated field. The header comment defers this as a follow-up, but until it's fixed this is a real last-writer-wins data-loss race on `bot-config.json`. Fold `TUNING_WRITE_LOCK` into `CONFIG_WRITE_LOCK`, or use a single shared lock for the whole config file.

Mutex poisoning recovery silently absorbs panics from concurrent writers. If a thread panics inside the RMW window (during `store.load()`, `db::prepare_for_upsert`, the field mutations, or `store.upsert()`), the next writer calling `e.into_inner()` proceeds as if nothing happened. Each thread re-loads from DB so data is not directly corrupted, but the original panic is swallowed, the root-cause bug is hidden, and the same panic will recur on every subsequent request - turning a recoverable bug into an indefinite silent degradation. Treat poisoning as a hard failure (return 500 / `Err(...)` out of the labeled block) so it is visible to operators and to the calling handler instead of masked by an `eprintln!` line.

Note: this pattern is repeated identically in `update_task` and `delete_task`; the same fix should be applied to all three call sites.

Static array indexed by `slot.index()` panics if any future `KeySlot` variant maps to an index >= 3. `KeySlot::index()` in `types.rs` currently returns 0/1/2 for Llm/Tavily/Brave, but that invariant is implicit — adding a fourth variant will compile cleanly and then panic at runtime the first time `migrate_legacy_keyring_entry` runs. Consider replacing the hardcoded `[AtomicBool; 3]` with a `HashMap<KeySlot, AtomicBool>` or attaching the migrated flag to the slot itself, and assert in tests that the array length matches the variant count.

Shutdown can miss a concurrently connecting client. `sse_connect` publishes its sender into `hub.clients` before acquiring `SSE_WRITERS`, while this function releases the registry lock before setting any stop flags. A request already dispatched by the accept thread can therefore register after this scan and keep the retired hub (and itself) alive indefinitely. Use a lifecycle gate shared by client admission and writer registration, mark the hub as stopping under that gate, and set all flags before releasing it.

`debug_assert!` for lock invariants is compiled out under `--release`. Recovery from `TryLockError::Poisoned` silently reuses the inner guard and continues. A poisoned mutex almost always means the previous holder panicked — silently swallowing that masks real bugs (state corruption, partial writes during the panic). Use `lock()`/`try_lock()` only on a recovered-from-poison mutex after an explicit audit event so the corruption is observable, and avoid keeping the inner guard if you can't prove the protected state is still consistent.

Lost-update race: `bot_set_active_model` does an unlocked load → modify → write. Verification-flag injection via full config replacement: `prune_verified_vendors` never checks `disk.verified_vendors.contains(v)`. The retain closure only verifies that the vendor's (protocol, base_url) signature is consistent between incoming and disk, so any vendor the frontend includes in `incoming.verified_vendors` whose entries already match in both maps will survive — even if it was never tested. Non-atomic credential/config coordination. In `bot_set_config` all keyring writes (api_key, vendor_key, tavily/brave) run *before* `lock_config_write()` and `write_bot_config_file_locked`, so a config-write failure or a concurrent save leaves credentials already changed while `verified_vendors`/config still describe the old state — the opposite of the documented fail-closed intent. `bot_clear_vendor_key` then separately updates `verified_vendors` and deletes the key without any cross-lock, so an in-flight `bot_test_connection` that read the vendor key before deletion can complete after the delete and re-add the vendor to `verified_vendors`, leaving a vendor flagged verified with no key. Additionally `bot_clear_api_key` never invalidates `verified_vendors` for vendors that had no vendor-specific key and relied on the global fallback. Stage all credential mutations under the same config lock and gate verified-flag changes on the same epoch/keyring state used by the probe.

Credential-bearing probe trusts caller-supplied destination. `bot_test_connection` accepts arbitrary `base_url`, `api_format`, and `vendor` from the IPC caller, loads the matching stored credential (vendor key or global fallback), and attaches it as `Authorization: Bearer` / `x-api-key` to a GET against the caller-supplied URL. There is no scheme/host allow-list, no binding to the vendor's persisted endpoint, and `api_format` is only branched on the literal `"anthropic"` — any other value silently gets Bearer auth with no warning. A compromised renderer (or any untrusted IPC caller) can exfiltrate stored credentials to any host. Validate the URL (scheme, allow-listed host or at minimum non-loopback/non-link-local) and require `vendor`'s persisted base_url to match before attaching credentials; treat unknown `api_format` as an error rather than a default.

Keyring errors silently coerced to "no key". Both branches use `keyring::read_api_key().unwrap_or_default()`, discarding locked-keychain / permission-denied / backend-unavailable errors. This contradicts the project's own policy documented on `bot_get_config` ("keyring 真实故障透传 Err，不吞成未配置") and the doc-comment on this function ("全局主 key 读不到（未配置 / 故障）按无 key 探活"). The practical consequence: a locked keychain makes the probe send no credentials, the server returns 401, and `verified_vendors.retain(|x| x != v)` then incorrectly removes the vendor from the verified list — turning an actionable KeyringError into a false-negative authorization decision. Propagate the keyring error with `?` (matching `has_vendor_key`/`has_api_key` earlier in the file) and let the caller decide.

Also verify the `use_skill` exemption at lines 271/280 cannot indirectly execute a tool that the deny rule blocks.

Cancellation-/panic-unsafe call/return balance: `tool.call` is emitted at function entry but there is no RAII guard (or scoped future combinator) to ensure `tool.return` is written if the future is dropped/panicked during `ask_user_confirm`, the tool body, `execute_mcp_tool`, `trace_sink` recording, or `skill_on_step_post`. Today only the manually-listed early returns are paired; any other abrupt exit leaves a dangling call in the audit log and an inconsistent skill step state. Wrap the post-`tool.call` body in a guard that always emits a final `tool.return` (or use a `defer`-style helper) keyed by the trace's `tool_call_id`.

Sensitive data in audit previews: `args_preview` (tool.call), `preview` (tool.return), and `parse_args` stderr logging (escape_for_log(args,200)) persist up to 80/200 chars of tool input and output without redaction. Tools commonly handle file contents, secrets, tokens, URLs, or PII; writing them to bot.log leaks them to anyone with log access and to log shipping pipelines. Apply redaction (regex on key names, content-type allow/deny) at the `audit::write_event` boundary or strip previews for tools that touch credentials, and downgrade `parse_args` error logging to the structured audit channel so it can be redacted.

Result/Option mapped to misleading status: `commit_and_report` maps `db_upsert_for` errors to `ToolResult::ok` with empty `refs`. Any consumer that decides domain success from `result.status` (skill post-hook, future pipeline stages, UI caches, automation that polls) will treat failed persistence as committed; only the textual error and a single audit event flag the failure. Either return `ToolResult::warn`/`error` so the semantic outcome is observable, or change every `ToolResult::status` consumer to consult the audit stream/result text first.

Allowlist is not an execution boundary. `npx -y @scope/pkg`, `uvx pkg`, `docker run --mount /`, `python script.py` all run arbitrary code/containers; combined with attacker-controlled args (only length-bounded, not shape-checked), checking argv[0] alone gives no real protection. Either treat config as fully trusted or block dangerous arg patterns / use a tighter launcher registry.

`bot_effective_params` returns `CommandResult<...>` but the function unconditionally wraps in `Ok(...)`. Race: the check–remove–spawn–insert sequence is not serialized per server. Two concurrent callers (different cfg snapshots, or `call_tool` racing `reload_from_config`) can both pass the fingerprint gate, each spawn its own subprocess, and the second `slots().insert(...)` clobbers the first — or, worse, resurrects a server that reload already removed. The `mark_down` path (see comment below) can likewise overwrite a freshly reconnected slot for the same id. Add per-id in-flight guards (e.g. a `Mutex<HashMap<String, Arc<tokio::sync::Mutex<()>>>>`) or a generation counter on the slot that `ensure_connected`/`mark_down` re-check before mutating.

`mark_down` unconditionally overwrites whatever is in the slot. If a concurrent thread just reconnected with a different config (or the user removed/disabled the server), this stale failure writes `Down` over the fresh `Connected` slot or resurrects a server that should be gone — wiping out a working connection until the next reload. Gate `mark_down` on the slot's current fingerprint (and on the slot being present at all), or skip the write entirely when the slot is no longer "ours".

`Slot::Down` carries no fingerprint, so `ensure_connected`'s fast path can't tell whether the cached failure corresponds to the current `cfg`. Every retry respawns unconditionally even when nothing relevant changed, and `connected_service` cannot distinguish "stale failure" from "current failure" — which is also why `mark_down` overwrites blindly above. Add `fingerprint: u64` to `Down`, populate it on insertion, and have `ensure_connected` / `mark_down` re-check it under the per-id guard.

Silent argument-shape loss: `args.as_object().cloned()` returns `None` for any non-object JSON (array, string, bool, number). A caller passing the wrong shape therefore invokes the tool with no arguments — possibly triggering defaults, no-op behaviour, or side effects — instead of receiving a typed validation error. Reject non-object values explicitly, treating only JSON `null` (and the absence of `args`) as "no arguments".

Only `TransportClosed`/`TransportSend` mark the slot Down. The bare `Err(_)` branch (which includes timeouts and protocol-level errors) leaves the slot `Connected`, so subsequent `call_tool`/`list_all_tools` keep retrying against the same broken service until config changes or a transport-level error finally fires. Mark Down (subject to the fingerprint guard) on repeated protocol errors and on the first timeout, or at minimum force a disconnect+lazy reconnect when this branch is reached.

The comment says "unwrap 让其响亮暴露" (let it surface loudly) but the implementation silently recovers from poison via `unwrap_or_else(|e| e.into_inner())`. If a panic ever does occur inside a guarded section, the corrupted `HashMap` is then observed by every subsequent locker without any surface signal. Either change the call sites to `.lock().expect("McpManager slots poisoned")` (or `.unwrap()`) to match the documented intent, or update the comment to reflect that poison is intentionally tolerated and accept the resulting loss of invariants. The same contradiction appears in `stderr_ring`, `stderr_tail_snapshot`, and `prune_stderr`.

Arbitrary child stderr lines are concatenated into the error string returned by `ensure_connected`/`call_tool`, surfaced through `McpSlotStatus.error`, and recorded in audit events. A server can echo values from `cfg.env` / header tokens (or anything else) into stderr; this path neither redacts secrets nor restricts which consumer sees the diagnostic. Either sanitize the joined tail (strip `key=value`, bearer tokens, common credential patterns), or restrict stderr-tail visibility to dev / logs and document exactly which surfaces may see it.

The 20-line ring buffer caps only the line count, not the per-line byte size. `BufReader::lines()` allocates the entire line into memory and the loop ignores `next_line()` errors — so (a) a child emitting one very long line (or no `\n` at all) balloons `VecDeque` entries and the same bytes are then copied verbatim into `format_with_stderr_tail` / audit / IPC; (b) a non-UTF-8 byte sequence returns `Err` from `next_line()`, the loop terminates, and all subsequent stderr from that child is silently discarded. Truncate each entry (e.g. to 4 KiB) on push, and on the error path log + continue (or use `read_until(b'\n', ...)` with a max-buffer cap) instead of dropping the reader.

The HTTP branch delegates all egress protection to `http_url_is_public` and disables redirects, but `reqwest::Client::builder()` still honors `HTTP_PROXY`/`HTTPS_PROXY`/`NO_PROXY` by default, and the URL check is performed before `reqwest` resolves DNS. Confirm the helper (a) rejects DNS names that resolve to loopback / private / link-local addresses, including IPv4-mapped IPv6 (`::ffff:127.0.0.1`), and (b) the resolved peer is pinned against the URL host — otherwise DNS-rebinding can still hit a private address. Fallback for missing/unreadable vendor key may leak an unrelated vendor's credential into the override entry's base_url: `crate::bot::read_llm_key(api_provider, active_model_id, models_by_provider)` does NOT return the global main key — it first resolves the *currently active* model's vendor and uses that vendor's key (keyring.rs::read_llm_key ~640). So a per-card override whose vendor key fails to read (or never existed) gets the active vendor's key sent to the override entry's endpoint, which can be a different provider entirely. The comment "全局 key 兜底" is therefore inaccurate; use `crate::bot::read_api_key()` (or a small wrapper that explicitly walks vendor → global main key → vendor-of-selected-entry) instead.

`#[derive(Debug, Clone)]` on `ResolvedModel` exposes `api_key` (cleartext) through any future `dbg!` / `{:?}` / `unwrap()` panic message that includes this struct, and through log crates that auto-format Debug. `BotConfig` deliberately avoids `Debug` for this reason; `ResolvedModel` should redact `api_key` (custom Debug that prints `api_key: "<redacted, len=N>"`) or drop the derive. Combined with the fallback bug above, this is a realistic leak path.

Screenshot filename race: `chrono::Utc::now().timestamp_millis()` truncates to millisecond precision, so two concurrent `tool_screenshot` invocations within the same millisecond produce identical `wm-screen-<ts>.png` names and silently overwrite each other on disk. The later caller reports a path/file that no longer corresponds to its own screenshot (and any concurrent model consumption of the older path gets corrupt bytes). Append a sub-millisecond counter, atomic file create (`create_new`), or a random suffix to `screenshot_filename` so collisions cannot overwrite an existing artifact.

DNS rebinding / TOCTOU between validation and browser open: `ensure_public_http_url` resolves the host once and rejects loopback/private IPs, but the validated URL string is then handed to `app.opener().open_url`, where the OS browser performs its own (typically later) DNS lookup. An attacker-controlled DNS record that returns a public IP at validation time and a private/loopback IP at browser-open time will bypass the public-net gate and open an internal address. The sandbox comment promises "DNS 解析后拒绝本机/内网/保留地址", so this gap undermines that guarantee — pin the resolved IP into the URL or use a host allowlist/canonical name rather than relying on re-resolution by the browser.

If the function inspects the name for per-tool failure semantics (e.g., only flagging specific tools as failures, or excluding certain error-text-only results), passing "" silently misclassifies every tool result. The block currently has access to `tool_use_id`; the matched tool_use's `name` (from the `emitted_tool_use_ids` tracking step) should be threaded through so `tool_call_failed` gets the actual tool name it was designed to inspect. As-is, this is either a silent misclassification or a misuse of the audit API.

`existed` check OR's `is_dir` and `is_file`. If `canonical` resolves to a directory (e.g., user passes a directory path that survives `resolve_writable` because the parent is writable), `existed = true` triggers the "覆盖已存在文件" confirmation branch, then `atomic_write` fails with `IsADirectory` (an opaque IO error). The intent appears to be "is there an existing file to overwrite" — should be `is_file` only (and `resolve_writable` should arguably reject directory targets as a separate hardening).

Per-tool `Allow` ToolRuleAction bypasses the whitelist check **and** the `perm_mode` triage entirely — it only emits an audit log. In `resolve_with_perm`, an `allow` rule for any tool means the model can read **any** canonical-resolvable path (including symlink-resolved escapes that fall outside every whitelist dir) without user confirmation. The comment says "rule_allow = 单工具 yolo" so this appears intentional, but worth confirming: (a) rule persistence/sanitization is hardened, (b) rule auth requires the same trust level as `perm_mode=Yolo`, and (c) `Deny` rules should still take precedence over an `Allow` for a different tool if a future refactor reorders checks.

Same per-tool `Allow` bypass exists in the **write** path: a single `allow` rule for `edit_file` / `write_file` lets the model write to any path the OS resolves, completely sidestepping `writable_dirs` and the `ask_user_confirm` danger prompt. The "覆盖已存在文件" sub-prompt is also bypassed by an Allow rule because `existed` branch sits above this check (actually below — `resolve_writable` returns before the existed check, but the cover-prompt logic still runs and emits its own confirmation). Verify the comment "与读侧同语义" matches the actual UX: does the user expect a per-tool Allow to mean "no whitelist, no confirm, ever" for writes? If yes, document it; if no, also gate the cover-prompt behind `rule.allow`.

replans_used is logged as `plan.replans_used + 1` but never actually incremented inside `replan()` (function takes `&PlanState`, immutable). The caller must remember to bump `plan.replans_used` after a successful call. If the caller forgets, `MAX_REPLANS` is silently bypassed — exactly the failure-mode the constant exists to prevent. Either take `&mut PlanState` and increment here, or return the new count and force the caller to update atomically.

spawn_subagent_locked writes upsert_tasks then insert_subagent without a transaction. If insert_subagent fails after the card has been written (constraint violation, lock conflict, mid-call I/O error), the task card is left in Doing with no SubagentRow referencing it — the orphan card then drives check_subagent_locked / finalize_card_locked into their `TaskNotFound` branches and stays stuck in Doing forever. Wrap both writes in conn.transaction() the same way run_subagent's setup block already does, so commit/rollback is atomic.

cancel_subagent_locked does update_subagent_status then conditionally upsert_tasks (the Doing→Todo revert) without a transaction. If the second write fails after the row is already Cancelled, the subagent row says Cancelled but the card stays in Doing, leaving the front-end a stuck 'in-progress' card and confusing the watcher / auto-finalize paths that key off card.column. Same fix as the spawn core: wrap both writes in a single conn.transaction() so they commit together or roll back together.

Mutex poison recovery via `e.into_inner()` silently discards the panic context. If a thread panicked while mutating the protected HashSet (or while holding DB_WRITE_LOCK mid-transaction), the in-memory state may be inconsistent yet every subsequent caller proceeds as if the lock were healthy — the same swallow pattern is repeated in ChatGuard::acquire/drop, ExecGuard::acquire/drop, chat_guard_is_held, create_exec_session, and persist_exec_reply. At minimum propagate the poison (return Err or re-panic) so the inconsistency surfaces, or document an explicit invariant that the protected state is recoverable after a panic.
Same poison-swallowing pattern as ChatGuard; a panicked writer leaves the running set in an undefined state and acquire/drop will silently keep operating on it.

DB_WRITE_LOCK is a global writer mutex; a panic mid-write poisons it and `e.into_inner()` recovers the lock without aborting the in-flight SQL transaction the panicking thread may have left half-done. Subsequent transactions inside this guard will then operate against potentially corrupted rows. Wrap the transaction in a `Transaction::set_rollback_on_drop` style guard and let the poison propagate instead of swallowing it.

`chat_execute_tasks` runs every supplied task_id sequentially with no per-task or overall timeout. Each iteration can invoke up to 50 rounds of LLM with full tool execution, and the only stop check sits between cards. A long batch combined with slow skills will occupy the runtime worker indefinitely and `/stop` cannot interrupt a card already in flight. Cap `task_ids.len()` at the call sites, wrap each per-card call in `tokio::time::timeout`, and consider a global deadline.

`bot_chat` has no function-level deadline. Only individual HTTP requests inside `run_model_loop` carry timeouts; the plan generator, memory injection, history-truncate-and-summarize call, image attachment, and any awaited LLM step can each stall indefinitely. While ChatGuard is held this also blocks the user's session from making further progress. Wrap the orchestration body in `tokio::time::timeout` and surface a typed `CommandError` on expiry so the caller can react and the guards still drop.

`register_exec_session` and `register_ask_context` are paired with explicit unregister calls on the normal return path, but neither has a Drop-based counterpart. A panic (or any future `?` added between registration and unregister) leaks the `sid -> origin` mapping in `AppState` for the rest of the process lifetime, and stale ask contexts will let `ask_user` fire from already-failed runs. Wrap both in small RAII guards so cleanup runs on panic/early-return paths.

The `find("\n}\n")` boundary finder matches the first `}` at column 0 after the function header — but the body of `run_python` (and `py_gate_acquire_inner`) almost certainly contains nested matches/closures/helpers whose closing brace is at column 0. Truncating at that brace silently shortens the inspected region: if `py_gate_acquire()` happens to be called after a nested `}`, the assertion passes for the wrong reason; if the call is moved past such a brace the test falsely reports a regression. Use a brace-depth counter, or `syn`-based parsing, to locate the matching `}` of the function header.

Blocking filesystem + DB I/O inside async `build_skill_block_for`. The leading comment claims "重活包 spawn_blocking" but the very first statement `let all = scan_skills(app);` performs a synchronous directory walk over all skills (and a `crate::db::open_db` + `load_all_skill_outcomes`) on the async runtime thread before the ONNX rank step is wrapped in `spawn_blocking_map`. This stalls the Tokio worker for the entire scan, which is exactly what `spawn_blocking` exists to avoid. Wrap the scan (or the whole `enabled` collection step) in `spawn_blocking` and `await` its result, then continue with the rank step.

Global `cfg` is used for reasoning model/provider instead of the resolved override. `model_for_reasoning` and `provider` (passed to `ReasoningEffort::resolve`) come from the global config, but when `model_override` is set, the actual request goes to `resolved.model`/`resolved.api_provider`. Reasoning effort mapping (OpenAiEffort vs AnthropicBudget vs GlmThinking) is model-family-specific, so resolving against the wrong model can produce the wrong reasoning wire flavor — e.g. an Anthropic override could end up sending a `reasoning_effort` field (OpenAI-only), and a GLM/o-series override could get the wrong budget gate. Use `resolved.as_ref().map(|r| r.model.clone()).unwrap_or(cfg.model.clone())` for `model_for_reasoning`, and use the resolved provider for reasoning resolution too.

Reasoning injection does not gate OpenAiEffort/GlmThinking by provider. The match on `http.reasoning` writes `reasoning_effort` and `thinking` blocks without checking `http.provider`. If reasoning was resolved as `OpenAiEffort` (e.g. for an OpenAI model) but the actual request goes to an Anthropic gateway (via override), an unrecognized `reasoning_effort` field is sent → risk of strict-gateway 400. Conversely, `AnthropicBudget` is gated to provider==Anthropic and silently dropped on Openai requests (which is correct, but the asymmetric handling for the other two flavors is the bug). Add provider guards like the existing Anthropic one.

Soft-warn remaining-budget message is mis-computed. The injected system message tells the model it still has `fuse_cap - soft_warn_at` calls left, but `function_calls_total` is already `>= soft_warn_at` at the moment of injection (the gate is `function_calls_total >= soft_warn_at`), so the true remaining budget is `fuse_cap - function_calls_total`. Misleads the model into thinking it has more capacity than it does, defeating the soft-warn's purpose of forcing convergence before the hard fuse (especially with low caps or after several rounds of in-flight calls).

Expired `at:` tasks still execute. `stale_ids` is computed from the same `all` snapshot that feeds `due`, and `classify_due` returns `Run` for any past `at:` with `sched_last = None` (the `at_expired` branch is not consulted here). The "stale cleanup" block runs *after* `due` is returned, so the scheduler has already spawned `run_scheduled` for the expired task by the time the schedule is cleared. This directly violates the documented invariant "防重启后补跑过期任务" and the test comment that `at_expired` is responsible for cleanup. The `due` filter (or `classify_due` for `at:`) must consult `at_expired` and exclude such tasks, or the cleanup must run before dispatch.

Stale/missed cleanup defeats optimistic locking by resetting `expected_updated_at` to the freshly-loaded row's own `updated_at`. CAS is bypassed, so any concurrent edit between the initial `db_load` and the cleanup `db_load` (e.g. user changes `schedule` from a past `at:` to a future `at:`, or updates `sched_last` after a manual run) is silently clobbered: the schedule is force-cleared or `sched_last` is force-advanced. Workflow and job update paths correctly use the original row's `expected_updated_at`; the task path should do the same (carry `expected_updated_at = t.updated_at` from the first snapshot through to the upsert).

One-shot workflow `at:` is stranded on any non-Ok path. `sched_last` is recorded before `workflow_run` is called, and the schedule is only cleared on `Ok(_)`. When `workflow_run` returns `Err` (busy / DB error / invalid state), the function falls through the `Err` arm, which only writes an audit log. The row is now `sched_last = Some(...)` with a past `at:` schedule: `at_expired` returns `false` (because `sched_last` is `Some`), and `classify_due` for a past `at:` with `sched_last` set returns `NotDue`. The `at:` workflow is never retried and never cleaned up — silently dropped. On panic, runtime shutdown, or cancellation between the `sched_last` write and the clear call, the same stranding occurs. Add a matching `Err` cleanup, and consider rolling `sched_last` back if the `Ok` clear fails.

`finalize_job_run` silently discards every write it performs. The three DB calls (`record_job_run`, `update_job_run_state`, `delete_job_row`) and the auto-pause notification are all unchecked. Concrete consequences: (1) `record_job_run` failure means no history row exists even though the UI assumes it does; (2) `update_job_run_state` failure means `retry_at`/`retry_count`/`enabled` are not persisted, so a job that the function reports as "已排重试" or "已自动暂停" actually has none of those changes applied; (3) `delete_job_row` failure on an `at:` job leaves the row behind forever (combined with the stranding window above); (4) `delete_job_row` is unguarded — it does not respect the original `updated_at`, so a concurrent edit during a long LLM run (the original `job` snapshot is used) is unconditionally erased. At minimum, log every error with `audit_log`; ideally add CAS by `updated_at` for the `at:` delete and a fallback rollback if state persistence fails.

Frontmatter delimiters are matched as substrings rather than line-bounded fences: opening `strip_prefix("---")` accepts `---foo` and closing `body.find("\n---")` stops at the first newline followed by any `---` (e.g. a description or example value containing the literal `\n---`). When this happens, `intents` / `allowed_tools` / `params` are silently lost, mode falls back to the default, and the risk-derivation rule (low → auto) may flip execution semantics with no diagnostic. Anchor the delimiters to lines consisting solely of `---` (allow optional trailing whitespace) before slicing.

`strip_frontmatter` reuses the same substring match: `body.find("\n---")` plus `body[end + 4..]` will also mis-terminate when content contains `\n---`, and will leave any trailing characters on the closing delimiter (e.g. `---abc`) in the returned body. Use line-anchored matching identical to `parse_meta` so both functions agree on what counts as the end of frontmatter.

content: Mutex poison recovery silently discards panic evidence. `e.into_inner()` returns the inner `MutexGuard` and clears the poison flag, so a subsequent panic that occurred mid-transaction (e.g., inside the INSERT loop) leaves the next caller proceeding against a DB whose state may be inconsistent (rusqlite's `Drop` for `Transaction` will roll back the in-flight tx, but nothing surfaces that to the caller). Because `_g` is held across `open_db` *and* the SQL transaction, a panic anywhere in this scope produces this risk. Prefer propagating `PoisonError` (return as a `CommandError`), or at minimum set a process-wide "db dirty" flag and refuse further writes until a checkpoint. Both `bot_history_save` and `bot_history_clear` have this same pattern.

The test "rank_skills_truncates_to_top_k_and_keeps_rest" does not actually verify the truncation or tail-ordering contract — it only asserts `out.len() == 7` in both the empty-query fallback and the "ranked" path. Worse, `rank_skills("任务", ...)` calls the real `crate::memory::embed::embed_text` rather than the fake, so the assertion relies on ONNX being initialized for tests and the comment "借用 fake embed 全命中" is misleading. This contradicts the module-level claim "测试：embed_fn 注入式设计，不依赖 ONNX." A regression in (a) the top-K similarity ordering, (b) the tail sort-by-name, or (c) the count of expanded vs. collapsed entries would all silently pass. Recommend refactoring `rank_skills` (or adding an `#[cfg(test)]` sibling) to accept an injectable embed closure so the production logic is exercised deterministically.

`sort_by` is unstable, and entries whose `embed(d)` failed all share the sentinel score. When the embedding backend degrades so that two or more descriptions fail (worst case: every `embed(d)` fails), the relative order of the tied entries — and therefore the contents of the "top-K" slice returned by `rank_skills` — is non-deterministic. The documented degradation contract ("引擎不可用 / query 为空 → None（调用方回退原顺序）") is therefore violated: callers receive a shuffled slice of the top-K rather than the original order. Either (a) treat `rank_indices` as "all-embeddings-failed ⇒ return None" so `rank_skills` falls back to the unmodified input as documented, or (b) use a stable sort with the original index as a secondary key so the fallback preserves input order.

content: Rollback window has no RAII guard: `reopen_failed_run_for_rollback` flips a `Failed` run to `Running` and trusts the caller to invoke `restore_failed_run_after_rollback` later. If the rollback segment panics, returns early, or the surrounding future is dropped, the run is left in `Running` forever — `active_skill_run_for` will return it, the main loop will silently advance a run that should be terminal, and the state-machine invariant (`Running` ↔ tool execution allowed) is broken. Wrap the open/restore pair in a small RAII guard (e.g. `struct RollbackGuard { ... }` whose `Drop` calls `restore_failed_run_after_rollback`) so any panic path is closed safely.

Registry keying is `name` but every accessor filters by `session_id`. Two sessions cannot run a skill of the same name concurrently: the second session's call to `active_skill_run_for` will either pick up the first session's still-active run (and the main loop will drive the wrong session's tool execution) or see a terminal run that the second session didn't start. Either key the map by `(name, session_id)` (composite key or separate per-session maps) or assert in `active_skill_run_for` that only one matching run exists per session_id, to make the cross-session collision detectable instead of silent.

Production test hooks `test_hook_insert_skill_run` / `test_hook_remove_skill_run` / `test_hook_skill_run_state` are `pub fn` with only `#[doc(hidden)]` and are not gated by `#[cfg(test)]`. The cfg-gated `test_insert_skill_run` / `test_remove_skill_run` / `test_skill_run_state` helpers right below suggest the intent was for both to be test-only. Accidental production use (or a buggy / malicious caller) silently inserts or removes live `SkillRun` records and corrupts the global registry. Gate them with `#[cfg(any(test, feature = "skill-test-hooks"))]` (or move the integration-test callsites onto the `#[cfg(test)]` helpers if they share a single test target) and gate the feature flag in `Cargo.toml`.

Silent mutex-poison recovery on `DB_WRITE_LOCK`: a prior holder that panicked mid-SQL would leave the in-DB state (or surrounding invariants) potentially inconsistent, but the recovery via `into_inner()` discards the panic signal and lets subsequent writers proceed as if the critical section was clean. After a poison it would be safer to either bubble the original poison error to the caller, return a typed `CommandError::LockPoisoned`, or run an integrity check before continuing. The same pattern is repeated in `bot_session_delete` (lines 124-127) and `bot_session_rename` (lines 147-150).

Async/sync mismatch on blocking DB writes: `bot_session_create` and `bot_session_rename` are synchronous `#[tauri::command]` functions that open a SQLite connection and run INSERT/UPDATE under `DB_WRITE_LOCK` on the calling (main) thread, while `bot_session_delete` correctly uses `spawn_blocking`. Under contention these sync writers stall the Tauri main thread, block UI events, and serialize behind `open_db` disk I/O. Consider making create/rename `async` with `spawn_blocking` (or wrapping the whole flow in `spawn_blocking`) so they match the delete path.

Critical panic: when caller passes no `params` (or a non-object value like an array/string), `params = serde_json::Value::Null` is assigned, but the loop at lines 80-86 then indexes into it via `params[&p.key] = ...`. serde_json::Value's IndexMut panics with "cannot access a Null with an index" if the skill declares any param with a default (or even any provided key). Net effect: every `use_skill` call without `params` against a skill that has defaults panics the caller; this is the normal case (model may legitimately omit params). Initialize as an empty Object instead: `params = match params { Value::Object(m) => Value::Object(m), _ => Value::Object(Map::new()) };`

All `start_skill` errors (disabled/blacklist/conflict/missing-required-params) are surfaced as `ToolResult::ok(e, ...)`. The harness / main loop therefore cannot structurally distinguish a refused skill from a successful load — it sees the same OK envelope and the same Vec<UI artifact> shape, and the only signal is a Chinese error string inside the payload. If anything downstream ever branches on the success flag (e.g. stop-the-loop, redact prior tool history, mark turn as failed), it will silently treat refusal as success. Either propagate a typed `Err`/`ToolResult::err`, or at minimum return a distinct envelope (e.g. a leading sentinel like `__skill_load_error__:…`) so callers can match without parsing prose.

Audit-trail gap: this `find` filters on `state == Running` only. The step counter was already incremented by `step_check` (which only checks for `Paused`), so any state change between `step_check` and this post-hook — e.g. user /stop causing a concurrent `skill_finish` → `Terminated`, or `step_check` itself flipping `state` to `Failed` for max-steps/timeout — silently drops the failure record, the `actions` entry for this tool, and the post-execute state transition (so the `is_fail` branch never runs even when the tool errored). Net result: `step` is incremented, but neither an `actions[]` entry nor a `skill_step_fail` line is written, and the skill remains in whatever state the other path set, not necessarily Failed. Either widen the filter to `(Running || Paused)` and only run the state transition if `Running`, or always record an audit line for the step (success/fail) regardless of terminal state.

`apply_conn_pragmas` discards the PRAGMA result rows. `journal_mode=WAL` and `synchronous=NORMAL` both return a row whose value is the *actual* mode that took effect; if WAL cannot be set (e.g. on a network FS, read-only mount, or when the file is not yet committed by another writer) the connection silently keeps the previous journal mode and the durability invariants the rest of the migration module relies on are violated without any signal. Run each PRAGMA via `query_row` and assert the returned value (e.g. `journal_mode == "wal"`), or at minimum log/return an error when the mode does not match.

`migrate_legacy_file_bindings` materializes the candidate rows via a plain `prepare`/`query_map`/`collect` and only afterwards calls `conn.transaction()`. The `SELECT` runs in an implicit read that is **not** part of the transaction's snapshot, so a concurrent writer that toggles a row's `files` column between the read and the `UPDATE` will either cause a duplicate `files` JSON write or cause the migration to miss a row whose `file_path` was just cleared — both break the idempotency guarantee this function advertises. Open the transaction first, prepare + execute the SELECT inside it (or use `BEGIN IMMEDIATE`), then iterate.

`migrate_data_json_file` swallows every failure (`read_to_string`, `from_str`, `prepare`, `query_map`, `transaction`, `upsert_tasks`, `commit`) as a bare `return false`, and the caller `migrate_data_json` does `let _ = migrate_data_json_file(...)`. Result: a corrupt or partially-written `data.json` is silently left in place, but a JSON that deserializes but fails to upsert also leaves the file intact with no log line, no error to surface, and no signal to the user that their data wasn't migrated. This is a real data-loss hazard. At minimum, log the underlying error (`eprintln!`, `log::warn!`, or whatever the project uses) on every `Err` path, and have `migrate_data_json` return a `Result<(), String>` so the caller can react.

Every rusqlite error is collapsed through `.map_err(|e| e.to_string())`, discarding the typed `rusqlite::Error` (SQL state, error code, chained context) at the API boundary. The pattern is repeated in `ensure_brief_entries`, `brief_list_global`, `brief_list_card`, `brief_delete_workflow`, and `brief_delete_task` as well. Consider propagating `rusqlite::Error` (or a project error type) and converting at the Tauri command boundary with added context — that preserves the ability to match on constraint violations and log structured diagnostics.

content: TOCTOU race in `people_ensure_placeholder`: the `COUNT(*) ... WHERE id = ?1` check and the subsequent `people_upsert_entry` call are not executed atomically. A concurrent real upsert for the same id between the SELECT and the INSERT will leave `count == 0` in this transaction's view, after which the placeholder write of `"未知成员"` will silently overwrite the real `name` (and any `avatar`) — directly violating the documented "已知 id 不覆盖" guarantee. The intent is best expressed as a single atomic statement, e.g. `INSERT OR IGNORE INTO people (id, name, is_self, updated_at) VALUES (?1, '未知成员', 0, ?2)`, which removes the check-then-act window entirely.

`brief_list_card` filters only on `task_id` and `brief_delete_task` runs `DELETE ... WHERE task_id = ?1` without joining/filtering on `workflow_id`. This silently relies on task_ids being globally unique across workflows. If two workflows ever share a task_id (short IDs, reused handles, imported/restructured tasks, or simply a caller bug), `brief_for_injection` will leak one workflow's history into another's prompt and `brief_delete_task` will silently delete the wrong rows. Either add `AND workflow_id = ?2` to both queries and thread `workflow_id` through the API, or document and enforce a uniqueness invariant on task_id generation at the call sites. The test suite does not exercise a same-task-id-across-workflows scenario, so the regression would not be caught today.

content: Phase 2c rollback unconditionally removes db_path-wal and db_path-shm, but the early guard at function start only checks `db_path.exists()` for the main file. If -wal/-shm sidecars pre-existed at the target location (e.g., from a prior partial import or a crash leaving orphan sidecars), Phase 2a/2b overwrote them with tmp_wal/tmp_shm, and this rollback then destroys whatever was there — including the pre-existing data. Extend the guard to also reject when the target sidecars exist (and snapshot their existence so rollback only deletes files this call actually created). The same pattern exists in the Phase 2b rollback and is the root reason a "fail-closed" import can destroy sidecars the user never asked us to touch.

The docstring claims "rename 覆盖目标" (rename overwrites target), but `std::fs::rename` on Windows returns an error when the destination file already exists rather than overwriting it. `atomic_write` therefore silently fails to overwrite existing files on Windows, contradicting the documented contract. Import/upgrade flows that depend on overwriting an existing file will fail closed on Windows for an entirely different reason than intended, and the file system will keep stale contents. Use a platform-aware atomic rename (e.g. Win32 `MoveFileExW` with `MOVEFILE_REPLACE_EXISTING`) or a dedicated crate that normalizes atomic-rename semantics.
`record_job_run` 的 INSERT 与裁剪 DELETE 分两次 `conn.execute()` 调用，未包裹在 `conn.transaction()` 中。若中间 panic、磁盘满或进程被中断，`scheduled_job_runs` 将无界增长，裁剪逻辑失效。建议在事务中执行：先 INSERT、再 DELETE，最后 `tx.commit()`。

`migrate_legacy_task_schedules` 在循环中执行多条 INSERT，最后一次性 UPDATE tasks.schedule/sched_last/enabled，全程未用 `conn.transaction()`。崩溃/中断可能造成「任务卡 schedule 已清空但 scheduled_jobs 行未生成」的中间态，破坏迁移的幂等契约（即使重跑也找不回已清空的字段）。建议把所有写入包到事务里。

/stop 与 `bot_confirm_response` 竞争 confirm map：若响应线程先 `take_confirm` 取走条目，再 `bot_stop` 把对应 StopGuard 标志置位，已在 `tx` 中持有的 ConfirmReply 仍会被 `deliver_confirm` 发送给等待方，调用方（如 `tool_delete_task`）立刻执行危险动作而不再检查 stop——注释「/stop 后迟到的确认点击不再放行危险动作」在此场景下不成立。
`/stop` 在异步清理 `clear_for` 完成之前就把 `Result<(), String>` 返回给前端；若 clear_for 还未清完挂起的子任务确认，用户立刻发下一条消息，模型循环的 `has_pending_for(session_id)` 仍为 true，子任务继续执行——/stop 实际失效。
`active_execution_count` 在锁中毒时直接返回 0，导致 lib.rs 的退出清理 `wait_executions_drained` 误判「无在途执行」并立即返回，进程退出时仍可能存在持有 StopGuard 但还未 poll 停止标志的工作线程——drain 失去意义。

`registry.lock().map_err(...)` 一旦遇到中毒就返回 Err 并把 mutex 永远留在 poisoned 状态，后续每一次 /stop 都会得到相同的 Err，前端看到错误但 stop 表已无法继续恢复——与模块其它处 `unwrap_or_else(|e| e.into_inner())` 的恢复策略不一致（StopGuard::Drop / stop_all_executions / confirms 的取锁路径都采用 into_inner 恢复）。

Startup race: only the legacy copy is protected by `LEGACY_COPY_LOCK`. Subsequent DDL, check-then-add migrations, the orphan-session backfill, and the `bot_assigned` reset run without `DB_WRITE_LOCK` and outside any initialization transaction, so concurrent `open_db` calls can race PRAGMA-then-ALTER and startup can halt midway with partial schema/data state.

Fail-closed schema probes silently coerced: `PRAGMA table_info` failures are turned into `false` via `.unwrap_or(false)`, so on real errors (busy/corrupt) the code blindly executes `ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN`, and `SELECT COUNT(*) ... WHERE session_id IS NULL` failures become 0 and skip the bot-message session backfill instead of surfacing the database error.

Legacy DB resolution errors are discarded: `app.path().app_data_dir()` failure makes startup silently skip the legacy copy step and create a new empty database while leaving the user's existing data unmigrated.

Pre-transaction reads rely solely on debug_assert!: `load_workflow` and `load_tasks_by_workflow` run BEFORE the transaction is opened. The only enforcement that `lock_db_write()` is held is a `debug_assert!`, which is compiled out in release. If any future caller forgets `lock_db_write()`, the read-modify-write window becomes a real TOCTOU: the `kept_task_ids` baseline, `expected_updated_at`, and `created_at` snapshot could all be stale relative to a concurrent writer, and the transaction would still commit. Consider either making `holding_db_write()` a runtime check (or having `workflow_save_locked` acquire the lock itself and assert before/after), or move the snapshot reads inside the transaction.

Cycle sentinel silently deletes cycle-bearing nodes on next save. `task_fp_at` returns a unique `__cycle__:<id>` fingerprint for any existing task that's part of a cycle, which can never match a draft (drafts reject cycles up front in `draft_fingerprints`). The result: any workflow whose existing `tasks` graph contains a cycle (via data corruption, an external writer, or a future regression that lets cycles slip into storage) will have those nodes deleted on the next canvas save with no warning surfaced. Consider either: (a) propagating the cycle condition as a typed error/warning so the caller can choose how to handle it, (b) treating the cycle fingerprint as still matching so the user is forced to break the cycle deliberately, or (c) at minimum logging an `audit_event` so the silent data loss is observable.

The unknown‑tool compatibility gate is broken. `unknown_tool_names` returns a deduplicated set that mixes main steps *and* rollback steps, and the comparison `unknown.len() >= steps.len()` then misclassifies valid plans (e.g. duplicate unknown tools in main steps, or unknown tools only in the rollback segment). In addition, the gate only checks the static `tools_index()`, ignoring the MCP fallback in `dispatch`, so skills that rely on MCP tools are prematurely terminated. Fix by counting how many *main* steps reference unknown tools (not a deduplicated name set) and by consulting a list of known MCP tools before treating an unknown name as fatal.

The per‑step state lookup is session‑scoped only; if a different skill for the same session is started while this scheduler is still running, `active_skill_run_for` will return the new run and the remaining steps will be advanced against the wrong run, corrupting the state machine and audit trail. Filter by `name` (or otherwise bind to the specific `SkillRun`) just like the wrapper does for params/allowed_tools.

Non-atomic status transition: `load → check → UPDATE` happens across three separate SQLite statements with no transaction and an unconditional `WHERE id=?1`. Two concurrent connections (e.g. runner + cancel signal, or two runner retries) can both observe the same pre-transition state, both pass `transition_allowed`, and the later UPDATE will overwrite a terminal state/timestamps (Running→Succeeded then Running→Failed; or queued→running then queued→cancelled), defeating the stated terminal immutability and idempotent polling contract. Fix by wrapping the read/check/write in a transaction and using a conditional `UPDATE ... WHERE id=?1 AND status=?expected_from`, returning `Err` when affected-rows is 0 (treat as lost transition).

Over-broad same-state bypass: the `row.status != to` guard makes every self-loop permitted, including Queued→Queued and Running→Running, which `transition_allowed` and the `transition_table_rejects_illegal_moves` test classify as illegal. Additionally, `COALESCE(?5, error)` rewrites the `error` column on a nominal same-state retry, so "terminal facts cannot be rewritten" is violated for the failure reason (and `started_at` can be back-stamped on a Running→Running call when the existing row lacked one). Constrain the exception to terminal→terminal only and never overwrite `error` on a no-op re-entry.

Silent enum fallback hides DB corruption: unknown `status` strings are mapped to `SubagentStatus::Failed` and unknown `profile` to `SubagentProfile::General`, returning `Ok(row)` with a fabricated domain value. The caller's state machine, retry logic, and profile-based tool whitelist will then operate on invented state — a corrupted row can be reported as Failed (triggering false failure paths), and a corrupt profile silently broadens tool access via the General mapping. Surface the corruption as a typed error (or an `Unknown` variant) instead of silently coercing.

Budget-clamp contract is unenforced at the persistence boundary. `SubagentBudget::max_turns`/`max_tool_calls`/`max_wall_seconds` are public fields, `clamped()` is opt-in, and `insert_subagent` writes `budget_json` as an opaque `Option<String>` without parsing or clamping. A row constructed directly (bypassing the documented spawn/task_patch path) can persist `maxTurns=0`, `maxTurns=u32::MAX`, or any wall value, breaking the safety budget that downstream runner/dispatch enforcement depends on. Either accept a typed `SubagentBudget` (call `clamped()` inside `insert_subagent`) or store a parsed struct and reject out-of-range values at write time.

Regex only matches the hyphenated 36-char UUID, but production task tools (bot/tools.rs: `uuid::Uuid::new_v4().simple().to_string()`) emit 32 hex chars without hyphens. `extract_task_id` therefore returns `None` for real task output, so `${stepN.id}` placeholders never resolve against actual `CompletedStep` data. The comment also mislabels the pattern as "v4" — the version nibble is unconstrained. Accept both forms and drop the misleading v4 claim, or document the limitation explicitly.

The byte-level `in_quotes` check only treats the placeholder as inside a JSON string when both neighbouring bytes are `"`. Common templates fail this heuristic — e.g. `{"note":"prefix ${step1.result}"}` (prev byte `f`), `{"note":"${step1.result} suffix"}` (next byte ` `), or any literal preceded by `\\"` / `: ` — so the replacement is inserted raw. A result containing `"`, `\`, or a newline then corrupts `args_json`, and `parse_args` (bot/dispatch.rs) silently downgrades the call to `Null` args, which downstream tools may execute with missing/empty parameters. The adjacent-byte check is structurally insufficient for JSON; replace it with a true JSON-string scanner that tracks string state and escape sequences.
existing_code:
let in_quotes =
            m.start() > 0 && bytes[m.start() - 1] == b'"' && bytes.get(m.end()) == Some(&b'"');

content: Each substitution stage consumes the previous stage's output (params → nested → by-index → prev). A `${...}` sequence returned from a `params` value or from a step's `result` is therefore re-scanned by later passes, so `params` is not actually static and step results are not actually literal. Concretely, `params = {"title": "${step1.result}"}` (legal per the key validator in parse.rs) expands step1's output into the next tool's args, and a result containing `${prev.id}` / `${params.*}` is interpreted in subsequent rounds. This breaks the documented "互不干扰" / 静态参数 contract and can leak context into tool arguments. Resolve every placeholder against the ORIGINAL `text` in one combined pass and never feed inserted values back into another `replace_ctx` call.

The module's top-level comment declares the run grouping key as the composite `(workflow_id, run_started_at)`, but `wa_prune` selects and deletes by `run_started_at` alone (`SELECT DISTINCT run_started_at ... LIMIT ?`). This conflates runs from different workflows that happen to share a millisecond timestamp and lets the number of retained *runs* diverge from `keep_runs` (the query counts distinct timestamps, not distinct composite keys). It can also delete entries of an in-progress run for one workflow simply because an unrelated workflow started more recently. Use the composite key, e.g. `DELETE FROM workflow_audit WHERE (workflow_id, run_started_at) NOT IN (SELECT workflow_id, run_started_at FROM workflow_audit GROUP BY workflow_id, run_started_at ORDER BY MAX(created_at) DESC LIMIT ?1)`, or at minimum document and enforce the global-timestamp semantic intentionally.

`workflow_audit_export` reuses the display query's hard `limit = 500` cap and returns the truncated row count as if it were the full audit. For any workflow whose retained audit exceeds 500 entries (the retention default is only 20 *runs*; a single run can emit many events), the JSON file silently omits older events and the caller has no signal of truncation. Either stream the export, drop the cap, or include a `truncated: bool`/total-count field so the operator knows the archive is incomplete.
existing_code: let rows = wa_list(&conn, &wid2, 500).map_err(crate::error::CommandError::DbError)?;

content: The export path is validated in `spawn_blocking_map` but the actual `std::fs::write(&path, json)` runs synchronously on the async Tauri command. That (a) blocks the Tokio worker for the duration of the write proportional to JSON size and (b) creates a TOCTOU window: the destination can be replaced (e.g. symlink swap, file deleted/recreated) between the validation task and the write, so a write can land on a path that was never validated. Move the write into the same blocking task (open with `OpenOptions` + `write_all` after the path check, or pass the opened `File` handle across the spawn boundary) so validation and write are atomic relative to the caller and the runtime is not stalled.
existing_code: std::fs::write(&path, json).map_err(|e| crate::error::CommandError::from(e.to_string()))?;

content: Settings update writes three key/value pairs in separate autocommit statements; if a later write fails (e.g., DB I/O error after the first two succeed), earlier settings remain persisted while the command returns an error, leaving configuration in a partially-updated state. Wrap the writes (and the final read used to build the returned view) in a single `Connection::unchecked_transaction` so all keys succeed or none do.

Getters bypass the setter's normalization. `node_acceptance_enabled` treats any string except "0" as true (so "false", "no", or garbage values become true), and `audit_retention_runs` accepts any in-range `u32` because clamping happens only on writes. Pre-existing or externally modified rows, plus any schema migration or manual DB edit, can change runtime acceptance and pruning behavior despite the documented "5..=100 / '0'|'1'" invariants. Apply the same canonical encoding and clamp on the read path.

The catch-all `_` arms in `node_acceptance_enabled`, `audit_retention_runs`, and (less critically) `review_model_id` collapse genuine SQLite failures — missing table, locked DB, I/O errors — into the documented default. The header comment only justifies falling back for missing rows / parse failures, so storage faults masquerade as ordinary "user did not set this" and propagate silently through `settings_view`. Surface DB errors to the caller (or at least log them) so a broken store does not silently flip critical runtime behavior.

`wa_prune` runs after the new retention value is already committed; a cleanup failure is only printed via `eprintln`, so users receive a successful response while old audit records continue to exceed the requested retention. If retention is treated as a compliance/policy guarantee, this leaves the system in an inconsistent state. Either roll back the new retention when pruning fails, or propagate the prune error to the caller (and consider including it in the audit event).

The audit event records the raw submitted `audit_retention_runs` rather than the clamped value actually stored and applied (`r.audit_retention_runs`). A request of e.g. 1000 will be audited as 1000 even though the database and pruning used 100, producing an audit trail that does not reflect the system's effective configuration and can mislead compliance review. Log the effective value (or both `requested` and `effective`) so the audit log matches reality.
