                "auditRetention",
                audit_retention_runs
                    .map(|v| v.to_string())
                    .unwrap_or_else(|| "-".into()),
            ),

content: Mutex held across notification dispatch, audit log, and file I/O. The guard from `notify_state().lock()` spans `app.notification().builder()...show()` (which may involve IPC on macOS), `crate::bot::audit_log(...)` (likely disk write), and `save_state(app, state)` (file write). All blocking work is serialized behind a global mutex even though no current caller races for it — this is a fragile invariant and any one slow dispatch stalls the entire notifier. Consider dropping the lock between `plan_round` returning and the dispatch loop, or restructure state ownership so the heavy work happens outside the critical section (e.g., snapshot pending + flags, release lock, dispatch, re-acquire to write back).

Flag is set before notification delivery is confirmed. `plan_round` mutates `entry.h1 = true; entry.t0 = true` synchronously and returns the Pending; if the subsequent `notification().show()` fails (permission denied on macOS, Focus Assist / DND suppression on Windows, IPC error, transient system failure), the dedup flag is already set and the notification will never be retried. The audit log records the failure but the user receives nothing, with no backoff or retry path. Consider only marking the flag after a successful `show()` (i.e., move the flag mutation out of `plan_round` and apply it per-delivery inside `run_round`).

`workspace_import` lacks the path gate that `workspace_export` has. Compare with the export command which calls `crate::db::tasks::check_export_path_gate(path.clone()).await?` before any `fs` work — this command goes straight to `std::fs::read_to_string(&path)` with no allow-list/sandbox check, so any file readable by the app process can be deserialized and merged into the DB on demand from the frontend. Apply the same `check_export_path_gate` (or an import-symmetric equivalent) here before reading the file.

`LlmApiError.body_preview: String` is whatever the upstream LLM provider sent back (multi-KB HTML pages, vendor-internal headers, possible echoed auth headers, stack traces from gateways). It is then concatenated verbatim into `message()` and the JSON payload with no length cap, redaction, control-character stripping, or header-line filter, creating both an info-leak path to the frontend/toast/log and an unbounded allocation on a remote-controlled error path. Cap it to a small fixed budget (e.g. 1 KiB UTF-8-truncated) on construction, strip control bytes, and ideally drop well-known secret-bearing header patterns before storing.

/// 大模型 API 错误（HTTP 非 2xx）。`body_preview` 由构造侧截断/清洗，禁止直传上游原始字节。
    LlmApiError { status: u16, body_preview: String },

/// 大模型 API 错误（HTTP 非 2xx）
    LlmApiError { status: u16, body_preview: String },

content: Same `body_preview` concern on the `message()` rendering side: the body is interpolated raw into a user-facing string. Even with a bounded variant, the `format!` here must apply the same truncation/sanitization before interpolation, otherwise the frontend toast/log can still receive unsanitized content.

The blanket `From<String>` / `From<&str>` impls silently funnel every string-shaped error into `CommandError::Internal`, which (a) makes `recoverable=false` regardless of root cause, (b) loses every semantic code the rest of the file is built around, and (c) provides no compile-time nudge toward the precise variants. Combined with `From<CommandError> for String`, this enables a round-trip that erases all structure. The doc comment calls this a migration aid, but nothing (lint, deprecation, feature flag, audit test) prevents new code from using the shortcut, so once an Internal escapes into telemetry the original semantic (TaskNotFound / AuthMissing / BotDisabled / etc.) is permanently lost. Gate it behind `#[deprecated]` once migration is done, or remove the impls entirely and force call sites to spell out `CommandError::Internal(s)` / the precise variant.

`From<CommandError> for String` is a one-way lossy conversion that drops the stable code and recoverable flag and keeps only the human message. The doc comment acknowledges this and limits the use case to "tool→model boundary", but `From` impls are global and `?` will silently invoke this anywhere `Result<_, CommandError>` flows into `Result<_, String>`, erasing the very contract the rest of the file is built to enforce, with no compile-time guard. Prefer an explicit `into_message(self)` / `into_code(self)` API gated behind a feature flag, or at minimum `#[deprecated(note = "Lossy; use .code()/.message()/.is_recoverable() explicitly")]`.

TaskStatus's custom Deserialize borrows `&str` from the deserializer, but most JSON deserializers (serde_json::from_value used by Tauri's IPC argument pipeline, any owned-string visitor, and any reader that delivers escaped strings) cannot provide borrowed data and will reject valid statuses. The code comment in apply_task_patch explicitly acknowledges this limitation ("TaskStatus 的自定义 Deserialize 只支持借用字符串，from_value 走不通"). This breaks the IPC surface for db_upsert (Vec<Task>), the return value of db_load, and any import whose status field contains escaped unicode (e.g. "d\u006fing"). Fix by deserializing into an owned String first and parsing it: `let s = String::deserialize(de)?; s.parse().map_err(serde::de::Error::custom)`.

delete_non_self_locked issues a raw DELETE that bypasses the brief_entries cascade that delete_tasks explicitly documents as critical ("卡片档案级联（ critical——原实现泄漏 brief_entries 卡层行）"). Orphan brief_entries rows remain for every non-self task that this path deletes. Additionally, the SELECT-id then DELETE pattern is not wrapped in a transaction, so under any caller that bypasses the global write lock (and there is no runtime lock assertion here, only naming convention) the returned `ids` and the actual deleted rows can diverge. Wrap the SELECT+DELETE in a single transaction and either route through delete_tasks or invoke brief_delete_task for each selected id before/after the DELETE so the cascade is enforced.

let n = conn
        .execute(
            "DELETE FROM tasks WHERE owner_id IS NOT NULL AND owner_id != ?1",
            [self_pid],
        )
        .map_err(|e| CommandError::DbError(e.to_string()))?;
    Ok((n, ids))

content: check_export_path validates the *trimmed* path (so "/dir/foo.json " is validated as "/dir/foo.json"), but the callers in tasks_export/tasks_import pass the original untrimmed `path` to atomic_write/File::open. On Unix, trailing whitespace is a legal filename character, so a path with a trailing space passes the symlink-rejection check on the trimmed target while the actual file operated on is a different name — which can be a symlink to arbitrary content. The gate is also pure time-of-check; the actual open/write happens later in a different thread without O_NOFOLLOW or re-validation, so a symlink swap between gate and op also defeats the no-follow rule. Normalize and return the validated path from the gate (or strip and reuse), and reopen with O_NOFOLLOW + re-stat immediately before the file op.

load_tasks_by_workflow is documented as feeding workflow fingerprint diff/save, but the query lacks any ORDER BY clause. SQLite does not guarantee row order without ORDER BY, so the same DB state can produce different task orderings on different calls, producing nondeterministic fingerprints, spurious diffs, and broken change detection. load_all explicitly orders by `ord, rowid`; this function must mirror that (or use an appropriate workflow-scoped key).
existing_code: let sql = format!("{TASK_SELECT_COLS} WHERE workflow_id = ?1 AND deleted_at IS NULL");

content: upsert_tasks is a public API whose correctness contract — that the caller holds DB_WRITE_LOCK and that bulk writes are atomic — is enforced only by debug_assert!, which is compiled out in release builds. Any external caller can invoke it without the write lock, defeating the SELECT-then-INSERT lost-update guard. The same is true for the sibling "_locked" helpers (task_set_column_locked, task_patch_locked, task_reorder_locked, delete_non_self_locked, import_tasks_conn): the suffix is a naming convention, not a runtime check. Either narrow visibility to pub(crate) so the contract is enforced by the module boundary and review, or upgrade the assertion to a runtime check that returns Err when the lock is not held.

`apply_one` calls `store::load_all(conn)` and runs two linear scans of every memory row on each invocation. When called inside `apply_from_consolidation`'s per-proposal loop this becomes O(M*N) full-table scans plus 2*M extra sweeps. Either hoist the `load_all` into a single `OnceCell<HashMap<...>>`/batch prelude in `apply_from_consolidation` and reuse it across proposals, or replace with targeted SQL lookups (`find_by_key_tag` for the key check and a `SELECT ... WHERE kind='lesson' AND content = ?` for the content check) so each proposal does at most one indexed probe.

When `embed_text` returns `None`, `apply_one` is invoked with `embedding=None`, which makes `store::insert_item`'s cosine similarity merge gate inert. In that path a near-duplicate of `p.suggestion.text` against an existing foreign-keyed memory is never detected, so `ConflictRefused` is impossible and the lesson silently overwrites nothing — but the audit/apply path still records `Applied` and writes the ledger. The current `evolution.embed_failed` warn is not enough: either skip such proposals (don't apply at all) or surface them as a distinct `EmbeddingUnavailable` outcome so they cannot bypass the anti-hijack check.

`super::change::read_all(&cr_path).unwrap_or_default()` silently swallows IO/parse failures into an empty `rows`, so `unique_change_id_for` derives `chg-<pid>` (or similar) without seeing existing entries. The local `EVOLUTION_STORE_LOCK` only serializes within this process; another instance, the panel write path, or an external tool can still race. Result: collisions are only surfaced as an `append_change` error, and the apply has already counted the proposal as `Applied` in `report`. At minimum log the read failure and treat as a Warn audit, or hold the read-and-derive-inside-lock pattern with explicit error propagation.

TOCTOU race on the JSONL append path. `entry::read_all(&path)` is followed by per-iteration `entry::append(&path, &entry)` with no file locking, so two concurrent callers — e.g. `evolution::post_consolidation` racing with the "shadow 钩子" the doc comment explicitly says depends on this file — can both read the same baseline, both find no duplicate, and both append, silently breaking the dedup invariant that this whole function exists to enforce. Add a process-local `Mutex` (cheap, covers the same-process case the comment describes) or, better, an OS-level advisory lock (e.g. `fs2`/`fd-lock`) taken around the read–append window; failing that, re-read and dedup per-entry right before each append (still racy but at least narrows the window).

Partial-write semantics break the documented contract. If `entry::append` fails on the Nth proposal, entries 0..N-1 are already persisted on disk but the function returns `Err` with an incomplete `written` Vec (which is dropped at the `?`). The doc comment says "通知中心按此逐条落消息", so the caller (notification center) cannot tell which IDs were persisted: a naive retry can silently re-emit notifications for entries that already made it, and a naive rollback leaves the jsonl in a half-written state that may also trip the next call's `read_all`. Either build a tmp file in-memory and rename it onto `path` only after the whole batch succeeds (atomic-ish, also fixes the append-mid-line hazard), or document the partial-failure contract explicitly and return a typed error carrying the IDs that did get written.

evaluate_s2 unconditionally returns Allow and ignores the proposal (`_p`), so any proposal routed through this function — including irreversible ones — is approved. Safety relies entirely on an external caller-side filter that this function does not enforce or verify. Enforce the reversibility/impact invariant at the decision boundary itself (or at minimum, return a typed error/Result so callers must prove the pre-filter ran) rather than relying on a comment-documented invariant outside the API.

The loader honors externally configured `s2_active` even though evaluate_s2 is an allow-all placeholder. A misconfigured or tampered bot-config.json can flip the system into S2 and approve main-memory writes before any real policy exists. Either reject `s2_active` while the placeholder is in place, or require an explicit "policy_implemented" flag before honoring it.

This test explicitly asserts that high-impact proposals are approved by evaluate_s2. With the always-allow placeholder, any regression that removes the documented pre-filter would still pass. Add a test that exercises the irreversibility/impact guard at the actual decision boundary (or assert via a typed error/Result from evaluate_s2) so the safety invariant is enforced and verified, not just trusted.

rollback_count and pollution_survival_days assume each `mem_key` appears at most once in `applied` JSONL. Retries/reapplications silently inflate `rolled_back_total` (every absent row counts as a rollback) and `pollution_survival_days` only retains the last-seen timestamp per key in the HashMap. Either deduplicate by `mem_key` (keep latest `applied_at_ms`) or document that callers must guarantee uniqueness; current code has no enforcement and no test for this scenario.

Unchecked i64 subtraction `(now_ms - *at)` panics under overflow checks or wraps in release builds. Corrupted JSON with extreme timestamps can therefore yield a plausible positive age and pass the `days >= 0.0` guard, polluting the survival metric. Use `i64::checked_sub` (or `.saturating_sub`) and decide on a documented policy for invalid/future records (e.g. skip silently, but never let wrap survive).
existing_code: let days = (now_ms - *at) as f64 / 86_400_000.0;

content: behavior_deviation trusts callers to validate inputs and enforce coverage. (a) Empty `hit_fractions` is treated as perfect 1.0 average, masking missing feedback. (b) `f64` fractions are not range/finite-checked — NaN propagates through `(1.0 - NaN).clamp(0.0, 1.0)` returning NaN, and values outside [0,1] silently bias the result (clamped). (c) `case_total` is only a zero-guard, so a short slice silently drops cases from the mean. Either validate inputs at the API boundary (reject non-finite / out-of-range, require `hit_fractions.len() == case_total` and unique case ids) or convert to `Result` and let the caller fix the upstream contract.

Hard constraint ② (no sandbox bypass) depends entirely on the caller. `can_transition(Approved, Active)` unconditionally returns `true`, and `transition` does not consult any policy. The module doc itself flags this: "调用方忘记挂策略门 = skip-canary 硬约束失守". Every caller site that drives `Approved → Active` must independently consult a kill-switch / skip-canary config; this file provides no guard. Add an integration-level test (or a wrapper helper in this module) that asserts `transition(Approved, Active)` is rejected when the skip-canary flag is off, so the invariant cannot regress silently.
existing_code:
// Approved
        | (Approved, Canary)
        | (Approved, Active)         // skip-canary 配置
        | (Approved, Rejected)

content: `append()` opens with `OpenOptions::create(true).append(true)` but never calls `sync_all()` / `sync_data()` and performs no explicit inter-process locking. Two concurrent appenders (e.g. Tauri command handler and a background worker) can interleave bytes mid-line and produce unparseable jsonl; a crash between `write_all` and flush can leave a truncated final line that silently halves the last record on the next read. The "锁契约" comment defers to an external contract — there is no defensive check, fsync, or temp-file rename-to-append here, so a single missing lock at any call site silently corrupts the file. Consider `fs2`/`fd_lock` for advisory locking, or append-and-rename via a sibling temp file.

`ChangeStatus` is a bare 9-state enum with only `is_terminal()` / `as_str()`. There is no `can_transition_to(&self, next: ChangeStatus) -> bool` (or builder/setter enforcing one) — any caller can persist any state into any record. The 9-state machine contract (`Pending → Shadowing → ShadowPassed → Approved → Canary → Active`, with `Rejected` / `RolledBack` / `Expired` as terminals) lives only in doc comments. Nothing prevents e.g. `Active → Pending`, a backward jump after rollback, or `Expired → Active`. With a `Mutex<ChangeRecord>` + setter, or a simple `validate_transition` helper called at every write site, you can make these impossible states unrepresentable.

The "theoretically unreachable" fallback uses `chrono::Utc::now().timestamp_millis()`, which is **not guaranteed unique** within the same millisecond. Two concurrent callers (panel toggle / shadow / apply CR all route through this per the docstring) can both exhaust 2..=9999 in the same millisecond and produce the **identical** `chg-<pid>-<ms>` suffix — reintroducing the exact "二次回滚永久卡死" bug class this function exists to prevent. Use a process-local `AtomicU64` counter, a UUID suffix, or `rand` — anything monotonic or with collision-grade randomness.

content: The 14-day TTL is never enforced: this helper only stores a deadline, and the current production code does not read `expires_at_ms` to transition `Pooled` entries to `Expired` (or otherwise expire them). Consequently, every ordinary entry remains pooled indefinitely as well. Add an expiration predicate and invoke it on the production load/consume paths; computing the timestamp alone does not implement the documented TTL.

The production entry point `shadow_apply_for_batch_with_app` is the only production caller, but every `#[tokio::test]` in this module exercises only `shadow_apply_for_batch` with `new_for_test`. The S0/S1/S2 routing (`S2Active → evaluate_s2 → Allow/Block`), the in-lock dedup against `ChangeStatus::Pending|Shadowing|ShadowPassed`, `unique_change_id_for` derivation, the `spawn_blocking` window holding `lock_evolution_store`, and the `evolution.not_reversible / evolution.blocked / evolution.shadow_dedup_hit` audit branches are all uncovered. Given this is documented as the only production path and carries the documented safety invariants (「本入口是生产唯一入口」), a dedicated e2e covering at least one happy-path S0 batch, one S2 Block batch, one S2 Allow batch, and one `is_reversible=false` proposal is required.

Global `TOTAL_WRITES` / `FAILED_WRITES` are `static AtomicU64` shared by both `shadow_apply_for_batch` and `shadow_apply_for_batch_with_app`, never reset in production. The threshold check at the end of both functions uses `TOTAL_WRITES.load()` (cumulative ratio across all batches and across both call paths), so a single historical failure batch keeps the `evolution.shadow_warning` audit firing on every subsequent healthy batch (cumulative failed/total stays > 5% forever), and the very first batch can spuriously alert if the cumulative rate from earlier runs is already above threshold. The check should use per-batch counters (locally incremented, then compared against `FAILURE_THRESHOLD`) rather than the global atomics, or the atomics should be reset to zero on each batch's evaluation.

`shadow_apply_for_batch` is `pub async` but performs synchronous filesystem IO (`sink.write_change` → `change::append_change`, an `open + writeln` syscall) directly on the calling task without `spawn_blocking`. The doc comment correctly flags it as test-only, but `pub async` exposes it to any future caller on the Tauri async runtime, which would pin a tokio worker exactly the way `shadow_apply_for_batch_with_app`'s comment warns against. Either downgrade it to a non-`async` synchronous `fn`, make it `pub(crate)`/`#[cfg(test)]`-gated, or wrap the write in `spawn_blocking` so the invariant holds regardless of caller.

Timestamp validation: reversed windows are only debug-asserted, so release builds silently report metrics for an end-before-start observation window. Additionally, `now_ms - window_start_ms` and `now_ms - app.applied_at_ms` are direct i64 subtractions on externally-sourced timestamps; corrupted JSONL values (or extreme system clock skew) can overflow in release (wrapping) or panic in debug, producing wildly misleading metrics. The public `compute` API takes raw timestamps and should validate/reject reversed windows explicitly (returning a `Result` or saturating with a documented error) rather than relying on `debug_assert!` and a `.max(1.0)` floor.

Sub-day window normalization: `.max(1.0)` forces any duration below one day to behave as a 1-day window, contradicting the documented formula `proposals_in_window / days_in_window`. A 1-hour window with 100 proposals reports ~100/day (correct: ~2400/day). Either drop the clamp (the division is already safe since the debug_assert guards the lower bound) or compute with millisecond precision and surface the actual fractional days; the current code systematically underreports candidate generation for sub-day observation windows.
existing_code: let window_days = ((now_ms - window_start_ms) as f64 / 86_400_000.0).max(1.0);

content: Rate cohort / denominator mismatch: only `candidate_generation_rate` is filtered to the observation window. `approval_rate` divides `promoted_count` (all proposals, ever) by `proposal_total` (all proposals, ever), and `rollback_rate` divides `rolled_back_count` (all ChangeRecords, ever) by `promoted_count` (proposals, ever). When a proposal owns multiple ChangeRecords, `rollback_rate` can exceed 1.0, and the lifetime vs. window semantics are undocumented. Pick one cohort (window-scoped or lifetime) and apply it consistently to all four metrics; if lifetime is intentional, rename fields and document it.

Survival join key identity: applications are indexed only by `mem_key` and the first occurrence wins. `AppliedRecord` also carries `proposal_id`, and `ChangeRecord` carries `proposal_id` and `change_id` — yet none are used. When a `mem_key` is reused across proposals or re-applied, every active change sharing that key is attributed the first applied timestamp, skewing the survival average. Either join on `(proposal_id, change_id)`/application-event identity, or enforce uniqueness of `mem_key` at write time; relying on `iter().find`-equivalent "first match" semantics hides a real data-integrity hazard.

The 5-item cap is a raw input-order truncation, which lets a leading run of Low-impact Distill or Medium-impact Merge proposals starve High-impact Contradiction proposals that the severity model is supposed to surface. Test `derive_caps_at_five` only checks length, not impact ordering. Either sort/filter by `impact` before truncating (High > Medium > Low) or document explicitly that order is FIFO and severity is not considered.

Proposal IDs are computed by joining arbitrary `String` ids with a literal `|` separator and no escaping, so two distinct sets can produce identical hash input. Example: `ids=["a|b","c"]` and `ids=["a","b|c"]` both sort to `["a","b|c"]` (different sort orders!) — `["a","b|c"]` joined with `|` is `"a|b|c"`, and `["a|b","c"]` joined is also `"a|b|c"`. The same hazard applies to Contradiction: `keep="a", drop="b|c"` collides with `keep="a|b", drop="c"`. This silently collapses distinct candidates under dedup. Fix by length-prefixing each ref or using a separator that cannot appear in id strings (e.g. `\u{1F}`).
Same delimiter-collision hazard on the Contradiction branch. Two keep/drop pairs that differ only by where a `|` falls inside an id produce identical hash input and collide in dedup.

content: Segment ③ walks `mark_human_applied` using the `cr.status` captured back in segment ①, then unconditionally writes `changes[pos] = cr.clone()`. If another caller mutates the same CR during segment ②'s apply window (e.g., `rollback_change_locked` flips status to `RolledBack`, or shadow/auto-apply advances it past Pending), segment ③ will silently overwrite that external status and resurrect a rolled-back CR. The re-`load_changes` here only re-locates by `change_id` — it never copies the file-side `status` back into `cr` before calling `mark_human_applied`. Fix: after re-loading, take `cr.status = changes[pos].status` (or skip the transition path entirely) so the write-back reflects the freshest persisted state.

`delete_by_ids` runs first; if it succeeds and then `rollback_applied` errors, the source mem_items are already gone but the apply-side lesson (key_tag `evo:<id>`) is left orphaned. The function returns the partial count and the caller (`delete_inner`) writes the proposal/CR as deleted, then propagates the error — so the user sees a failure but the lesson is permanently orphaned (still surfaced via injection_block, referring to a deleted proposal). Either run `rollback_applied` first (lesson first, refs second; on lesson failure nothing is changed), or commit both inside a single SQLite transaction so a mid-failure rolls both back.

Step ordering in `delete_inner` deletes the proposal line and pending CR rows before the optional cascade_source runs. If cascade_source fails (DB locked, disk full, SQLite busy), the function returns Err but the proposal and CRs are already gone — the next retry returns "proposal {id} 不存在" while orphan mem_items (source refs + lesson) remain in the DB, and the user has no visible way to retry the cleanup. Either reorder so cascade runs before the jsonl rewrites, or make the cascade failure a non-fatal warning (log + propagate only the proposal/CR deletion result) since the orphan mem_items are still recoverable from the proposal_id key_tag.

DB_WRITE_LOCK held across the entire snapshot read. The mutex is acquired before open_db() and only released when the function returns, so every other DB-using caller (read or write) is blocked for the full duration of open_db + ensure_table + load_all. Holding a synchronous lock across I/O is also a cancellation hazard — if the surrounding task is dropped mid-query the lock is held until the JoinHandle is dropped without running the guard's Drop. For a read-only snapshot, prefer a short-lived lock just around the I/O call, or split into open + (lock + read + unlock) so other writers are not stalled.

Silent mutex poison recovery hides corruption. `e.into_inner()` after a poisoned MutexGuard unpoisons the lock and lets the function proceed as if the lock were healthy. The original panic may have occurred in the middle of a write transaction — at that point the on-disk state (or in-memory invariants protected by the same lock) can be inconsistent, and this recovery masks that fact from every later caller. At minimum, this should return an Err("mutex_poisoned") instead of forging ahead and emitting only an eprintln line.

The proposal_id is inserted into the 24h dedup map and `EmitReport.written` is incremented BEFORE the AppHandle is checked and BEFORE `audit_event!` is invoked. As a result, a startup-order mistake (AppHandle not yet registered) or any audit-side failure silently drops the audit row while the proposal is permanently suppressed from re-emission for 24 hours. The public API exposes no audit outcome; `EmitReport.written` reflects "claimed by dedup" not "audited". Consider either (a) inserting the dedup record only after a successful audit, (b) extending `EmitReport` with a `not_audited`/`audit_failed` counter and returning a Result, or (c) at minimum reverting the dedup claim in a catch path so retries remain possible until the audit actually succeeds.

Lost-update race: this is a separate process-local mutex from APPLY_POLICY_WRITE_LOCK at line 63, yet both `set_apply_policy_at` and `set_derive_thresholds_at` RMW the same `bot-config.json`. If a caller (e.g., settings page) toggles the policy while another path writes thresholds, both threads can read the same baseline, each modify a different field, and the later `atomic_write` silently overwrites the other setter's changes — even though each individual replacement is atomic. Replace the two locks with a single shared mutex (or per-file lock) covering every writer to that file.
existing_code: static DERIVE_THRESHOLDS_WRITE_LOCK: std::sync::Mutex<()> = std::sync::Mutex::new(());

content: Fail-open governance on any read error: only JSON parse failure is logged; every other `std::io::Error` from `read_to_string` (PermissionDenied, IsADirectory, transient antivirus/backup lock, broken symlink, etc.) is silently mapped to `ApplyPolicy::Auto`. A user who has explicitly selected `confirm` can have their governance choice silently bypassed by a transient filesystem hiccup. Same pattern at lines 119-125 for derive thresholds. Consider distinguishing "config truly unset" (default Auto) from "config present but unreadable" (preserve last-known or fail-closed) and surface all read errors via `eprintln!` for diagnosability.

Semantic contradiction with the documented header comment. The header says `all_auto_apply` only disables *automatic* apply and manual/human approval is still allowed, but `should_shadow_only()` is OR-true under `all_auto_apply`, so any downstream apply path that gates on `should_shadow_only()` (rather than on `should_auto_apply()` alone) will silently block the explicitly approved manual write too. Verify the manual apply entry only consults `should_auto_apply()`, or split the predicates so shadow-only and auto-suppression can be distinguished.

Safety-critical configuration is permissive by default and accepts unknown fields. `#[serde(default)]` makes every missing field `false` (i.e. automation on, notifications on, shadow off) and unknown keys such as `all_auto_aply` are silently ignored, so an operator typo or partial `kill_switch: {}` block silently re-enables automatic apply. For a kill-switch, consider `#[serde(deny_unknown_fields)]`, a typed constructor, or a validation step that fails closed on empty/typo'd input.

content: `read_all` 与 `append` / `rewrite_jsonl` 之间没有任何同步。多个调用点（如 `panel::commands::load_proposals`、`precompute_human_apply_embedding`）在没有持 `EVOLUTION_STORE_LOCK` 的情况下调用 `read_all`，若与 `append`/`rewrite_jsonl` 并发执行会读到正在写入的半行 JSON，`read_jsonl` 会把这种行当作损坏并把整文件备份为 `.corrupt`，导致正在追加的条目永久丢失。请在文档中明确该函数必须在 `EVOLUTION_STORE_LOCK` 持有下调用，或把公开 API 改为内部并集中加锁。

`c.to_ascii_lowercase()` only handles ASCII A-Z; non-ASCII uppercase letters (e.g. `Ä`, `É`, `Ω`, Cyrillic `М`) are returned unchanged. This silently breaks the documented "uppercase → lowercase" contract for any non-ASCII input — the same problem described with different casing/diacritics will produce different `proposal_id`s, defeating the cross-language dedup goal. The inline comment about `is_numeric` correctly switches to Unicode semantics, but the lowercasing branch did not. Either use `c.to_lowercase().next().unwrap_or(c)` (Unicode full-mapping) or apply `char::to_lowercase` and accept the iterator, and extend the test suite with cases such as `"Ä"` vs `"ä"` and `"É"` vs `"é"` to lock the behavior.

`is_reversible` is a coarse 2-rule predicate that ignores the actual mutation surface of the proposal. It returns `true` for any non-`ToolSchemaHint`/non-`High` proposal even when `Suggestion.structured_patch` is `Some(_)` (Phase 1 invariant is documented but not enforced at the type level — see `Suggestion` and its public `Option<String>`), and even when the target is `SkillDsl` or `MemoryPolicy`, which can rewrite executable DSL or persistent policy. Since shadow/activation routing "depends on it" (per the doc comment), a `true` here can authorize an irreversible action. Either include `structured_patch.is_none()` and target-kind checks in the predicate, return the patch-presence as a separate signal, or restrict the reversible branch via a newtype/constructor that statically forbids patches.

The doc comments assert a strict data-minimization contract ("**不**存原始堆栈 / 文件路径 / 用户输入" / "**不**存原始路径 / 对话内容"), but the fields are plain public `String`/`Vec<String>` with no validation, no newtype wrapping, and no constructor. Anyone constructing an `EvolutionProposal` (including a future `Deserialize` consumer if audit input is ever re-ingested) can persist absolute file paths, stack traces, or PII into the audit stream, and the type system will not complain. Either (a) wrap these fields in newtypes (`TraceId`, `ToolName`, `MemoryId`, `SanitizedSummary`) so callers cannot accidentally construct invalid values, or (b) add a validating constructor used by the audit writer that rejects/redacts the disallowed content before it ever reaches the public struct.

TOCTOU race + overwrite violate the documented "不覆盖" invariant. `backup.exists()` returning false does not guarantee another concurrent reader hasn't just created it (or is about to); `std::fs::copy` always overwrites the destination, so whichever caller's copy runs second clobbers the original forensic snapshot. Additionally, the copy is non-atomic with concurrent appends — the snapshot can capture an arbitrarily torn intermediate state. Use a single atomic `create_new` (open with `O_CREAT|O_EXCL` semantics, e.g. `OpenOptions::new().write(true).create_new(true)` + manual copy, or `fs::rename` after writing to a unique tempfile), or guard the whole "check + copy" sequence under the store lock that the file's writer holds.

format_candidates is unsafe for multiline content. Memory entries are free text and can contain '\n', which corrupts the `id | kind | importance | content` pipe-delimited format sent to the LLM. The LLM can then mis-attribute ids to contents and emit merge/contradiction/distill ops that target the wrong rows, which get applied to the DB. Replace newlines in m.content (and ideally also '|' collisions) before formatting, e.g. `m.content.replace('\n', " ").replace('\r', " ")`, or use a structured JSON/serde prompt instead of a plain-text pipe format.
existing_code:
fn format_candidates(items: &[MemItem]) -> String {
    items
        .iter()
        .map(|m| format!("{} | {} | {} | {}", m.id, m.kind, m.importance, m.content))
        .collect::<Vec<_>>()
        .join("\n")
}

content: gather_candidates loads the entire memory table into RAM on every tick. store::load_all is unbounded, then the OR-filter (updated_at_ms>=threshold || access_count>=N) is applied in memory before the LIMIT. Over months of use this becomes O(total_memories) per 10-minute tick, both CPU and heap. Push the WHERE clause into SQL (with the OR predicate) and apply LIMIT server-side; only fall back to in-memory filtering when an explicit ORDER BY + sort is needed.

Scheduler has no shutdown/cancellation and can overlap with manual runs. The spawned loop runs forever with no cancellation token, so on app exit it is dropped mid-LLM-call or mid-transaction (the inner spawn_blocking may still complete in background, producing orphaned DB writes). Independently, while the scheduler is awaiting run_consolidation (LLM call is not under DB_WRITE_LOCK), a manual memory_consolidate_now click issues a parallel LLM call against the same candidate snapshot — only the DB write path is serialized, so you waste API quota and can produce duplicate / interleaved ops that race at id resolution. Add a CancellationToken (or watch channel) the loop selects on alongside the ticker, and an in-flight flag (or DB-level advisory) to suppress the manual run while a scheduled run is active.

Mutex poison recovery masks state corruption: `e.into_inner()` after `eprintln!` silently continues with whatever state the panicking thread left behind in the `pending_map`. A panic while holding this lock (e.g. inside `park` after constructing `PendingExec`, or any future caller) means subsequent calls operate on a half-mutated map; the only signal is a stderr line. Consider returning `Result` (or panicking on poison) so the inconsistency surfaces instead of being silently absorbed — and do not duplicate the same recovery in three different functions.

Same `e.into_inner()` poison-recovery pattern is repeated in `park` and `take_pending_for`. Combined with the comment "（缺失时兜底实例）" on `pending_map`, a future contributor is likely to copy the pattern again. Centralize the locking into one helper (`fn with_pending_map<R, T>(app, f) -> T`) that either fails loudly on poison or returns `Result`, so the recovery decision is made in one place rather than silently masked at every lock site.

`pending_map(app)` is documented as returning a fallback instance when `AppState` is not managed. In production that means a fresh, throwaway `AppState` (and thus a throwaway pending map) is constructed on every call — `park` and `take_pending_for` end up writing/reading different maps, so pending state vanishes silently between calls. Either remove the fallback and panic/log loudly when `AppState` is missing, or have `pending_map` panic-once-and-cache so the bug is observable rather than invisible.

`mark_subtask_done` does a non-atomic load→mutate→upsert without verifying that the snapshot it loaded is still current: `expected_updated_at = t.updated_at` is set from the snapshot's own `updated_at`, not from the DB's current value, so `db_upsert` has no real baseline to check against and concurrent mutations (user toggling a different subtask during confirm) are silently overwritten. Additionally, a failed `db_upsert` only `audit_log`s and returns, so `advance_or_finish` proceeds as if the subtask was checked off and the next-step loop keeps moving. Either return `Result` so callers can react, or perform a proper compare-and-swap inside `db_upsert` using a fresh `expected_updated_at` read right before the write.

Gate whitelist uses `matches!` patterns on enums that are NOT `#[non_exhaustive]` (verified in `proposal.rs` lines 44-51 and 86-92: both `ProposalCategory` and `ImpactLevel` are plain enums). Adding a new variant — e.g. `ImpactLevel::Critical` or `ProposalCategory::LoggingHint` — will compile cleanly and silently reject the new variant (the `matches!` returns `false`), contradicting the doc's explicit "未来新增 impact 变体必须显式 opt-in" design intent. The type system will not flag missed updates. Consider marking both enums `#[non_exhaustive]` (forces update sites to be revisited), or — at minimum — adding a `#[test]` that asserts the patterns stay allow-lists (e.g. lock the discriminant count) so silent expansion is caught in CI.

Wall-clock forward jumps (NTP slew, manual clock adjustment, VM clock drift) inflate `duration_ms` and falsely trip the `> 60s` sampling rule. `saturating_sub` only neutralises negative durations; a forward jump of even a few minutes will over-record traces and distort audit signal. Consider clamping `duration_ms` to a sane upper bound before sampling, or capturing `started_at_ms` and `ended_at_ms` from a monotonic clock (`std::time::Instant`) for the duration measurement while still emitting the wall-clock timestamps in the audit record.
existing_code: let duration_ms = ended_at_ms.saturating_sub(ctx.started_at_ms);

content: Every failure path inside `embed_text` collapses to `None` via `.ok()?` with zero logging: tokenizer encode errors, `Tensor::from_array` allocation errors, `Mutex` poisoning, `session.run` ONNX errors, `try_extract_tensor` shape/type mismatches, and the manual `data.len() != seq * EMBED_DIM` check. In production this makes silent embedding degradation completely invisible — the memory subsystem will quietly fall back to keyword-only recall with no telemetry to explain why. At minimum, gate a `log::debug!`/`eprintln!` (consistent with the existing init-time `eprintln!` style) on each path so failures are diagnosable.

Mutex poisoning recovery silently continues after a prior panic. `e.into_inner()` returns the locked guard without clearing the poison flag, so if any prior task panicked mid-transaction (e.g. inside `apply_reflection`'s tx before `commit()`), subsequent operations proceed on potentially inconsistent DB state with no integrity check. Consider treating a poisoned `DB_WRITE_LOCK` as a hard error for write paths (return Err) and only allow recovery for read paths, or at minimum require an admin-initiated reset before resuming writes.

Check-then-act race violates the documented "same key 覆盖" invariant. `find_by_key_tag` followed by either `update_by_id` or `insert_item_with` runs outside any transaction; two concurrent `remember_fact` calls with the same key can both observe `Ok(None)` and both insert, producing duplicate rows whose `tags[0]` equals the same key. `insert_item_with`'s semantic dedup is by embedding cosine, not by `tags[0]`, so two near-identical simultaneous inserts bypass it. Either wrap find+update/insert in a transaction (with `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` to serialize writers) or enforce a UNIQUE index over `tags[0]` for fact kinds and surface the conflict error.

Data-loss bug: two extracted facts can both be judged `update` against the same existing memory, causing the first update to be silently overwritten by the second one. `plan_adjudication` runs independently per fact, so a top-1 candidate can appear for multiple facts; `parse_adjudication` only validates the per-index `existing_id` against the candidate and never checks that the same `existing_id` has already been claimed by an earlier entry. `apply_adjudications` then runs two `find_by_id` + `update_by_id` on the same id in order, clobbering the first fact's content/embedding. Track the set of update targets that have already been claimed in this batch and fall back to `New` on a duplicate (semantic dedup at insert time then either merges or inserts a new row, preserving both facts).

`meta_upsert_model` maps every error from `upsert_model_user` into `CommandError::DomainRule`, including genuine `rusqlite::Error` values (SQLITE_BUSY, disk I/O, constraint failures) that `upsert_model_user` flattens via `.to_string()`. Downstream the frontend treats all of these as user-facing domain-rule errors, hiding infrastructure failures behind a misleading `meta: <rusqlite msg>`. Split the typed error inside `upsert_model_user` (or return `rusqlite::Error` for DB paths) so DB failures flow through `CommandError::from` and reserve `DomainRule` for the provider-missing check only.

Credential migration prerequisites are not enforced: the comment requires `migrate_bot_config_schema` to run before the secret-clearing migrations, but each step only logs on Err and unconditionally runs the next. If schema migration fails, the subsequent `migrate_legacy_key` / `migrate_search_keys` may rewrite an unmigrated config and lose credentials. Gate later migrations on the schema migration's success or have them refuse to operate when the schema version is missing.

Cleanup is not a global admission gate: `stop_all_executions` only flags already-registered entries, the API is stopped afterward, and `bot_py::mark_exiting()` is invoked last. New API/scheduler work accepted between snapshot and `mark_exiting` is not in the snapshot and can spawn after `wait_executions_drained` returns, then be killed mid-write. Establish a single `app_exiting` flag set at the very start of cleanup, gate every producer on it, and check it inside `wait_executions_drained`/`mark_exiting`.

Nonessential widget creation is fatal after services are already launched: `setup` registers API state, AppState, MCP, scheduler, trace sink, due notifier, DB pruning, memory, migration polling, meta sync, MCP reload, etc., before `WebviewWindowBuilder::build()?`. A widget build failure propagates out of `setup`, the later `expect` panics, and `cleanup_on_exit` never runs because `RunEvent::ExitRequested` is not emitted. Either move the widget build before background service starts, or downgrade widget failure to a logged warning like the tray/shortcut paths.

content: Untrusted IPC path with no boundary validation: `copy_file_with_title` takes `path: String` straight from the frontend and forwards it to the native clipboard helper without canonicalization or scope checks here. Given the deliberate removal of frontend `opener:allow-open-path` (see the capability_tests comment about XSS and `$HOME/**`), the clipboard route must enforce that the path is bound to the calling task and resolve to an allowlisted root. Add a guard in this command or confirm the helper strictly rejects unbound paths.

16MB cap is enforced *after* the chunk is materialized. A single chunk larger than the cap (or many chunks each near-cap) is fully allocated before the check trips — OOM-by-network is still possible, defeating the comment's stated intent. Use `resp.take(MAX_BODY as u64)` (or `bytes_stream().take(...)`) so reqwest aborts reading once the cap is hit, and additionally reject any single chunk with `chunk.len() > MAX_BODY` to bound peak memory at roughly `2 * MAX_BODY`. The current `buf.len() + chunk.len() > MAX_BODY` check also can theoretically wrap on 32-bit targets if `chunk.len()` is large — `checked_add` or the `take()` approach removes that footgun.

Cancellation-safety hole: after fetch+parse succeed the DB write is dispatched to `spawn_blocking` and only its `JoinHandle` is awaited. If the outer future is dropped (caller cancellation, manual-sync command timeout, app shutdown), the spawned thread still runs `apply_sync` to completion — the caller can no longer report success/failure, and shutdown may race with the in-flight write. Either run `apply_sync` synchronously after parse (no `spawn_blocking`), or hold the JoinHandle and ensure shutdown awaits outstanding syncs before closing the DB. Dropping a `Vec<MetaProvider>`/`Vec<MetaModel>` after parse but before commit also discards the work, so this is genuinely fire-and-forget today.

A raw substring match is not a safe execution trigger. Messages such as `不要执行这些任务` or `暂时别运行` contain the trigger words and will directly execute the referenced cards. It also matches unrelated words and attachment paths (`/tmp/logo.png` contains `go`, and `.docx` contains `do`) because ASCII keywords are not word-bounded. Since this result bypasses the LLM and invokes batch task execution, require an explicit command/structured trigger and reject negated or incidental matches.

The parser treats the entire remainder of the message as the selected-task block. Because titles are nested inside this line-oriented format and may themselves contain line breaks, a title such as `Review\n- id=other，标题=...` injects an additional task ID; quoted text or a second example block after the marker has the same effect. Those IDs are then executed without going through the LLM. Use an escaped/structured payload (or an explicit end delimiter) and reject unexpected trailing content instead of scanning every later `- id=` line.

`decay_days` is a public `f64` with no validation. Zero produces `0.0/0.0 = NaN` for same-timestamp items (silently dropped by the `score > 0.0` filter); negative values invert the intended exponential decay and can overflow to `+inf`, letting a single item dominate ranking; `NaN`/`Inf` from upstream config corrupt every score. Either validate (`decay_days.is_finite() && decay_days > 0.0`) in `RankParams::of` or document and treat degenerate values explicitly (e.g. clamp the reciprocal).

`cosine(...).unwrap_or(0.0)` collapses every `None` to a legitimate zero similarity, while the later zero-match guard only checks `query_emb.is_none() || item.embedding.is_none()`. If `cosine` returns `None` for dimension mismatch, zero-norm vector, or non-finite embeddings (instead of "missing"), those items bypass the guard and can still receive positive `importance`/`recency` weights, breaking the documented "zero match → recent fallback" contract. Audit `cosine`'s `None` semantics and either widen the guard to mirror them or propagate the failure as a typed result.

content: `(now_ms - base) as f64` performs a raw `i64` subtraction on two caller-supplied timestamps. Extreme or corrupted values from persistent storage can overflow: debug builds panic, release builds wrap and the subsequent `max(0.0)` cannot recover the original magnitude, yielding meaningless ages (and `exp` values). Use `checked_sub`/`saturating_sub` and decide on an explicit policy for invalid ages.

TOCTOU race: src.exists()/d.exists() is checked in the main loop, then db_load → db_upsert runs inside `tauri::async_runtime::block_on`. Between the filesystem check and the upsert, a concurrent move/delete (user action, another migration) can make the repair write a stale or now-incorrect file_path. The `file_path_untouched` guard inside recover_move_db only protects against DB changes, not on-disk state. Consider re-checking `dst.exists()` after `db_load` (or holding the path inside the same transaction window) before calling db_upsert.

(Severity is high because recovery is supposed to be the source of truth that converges inconsistent state; a stale write would silently corrupt DB-to-disk correspondence.)

`tauri::async_runtime::block_on` is used inside `recover_move_db`/`recover_delete_db`. The comment claims these are only ever called from `spawn_polling`'s std::thread so block_on is safe, but that contract is not enforced at this layer—`journal_replay_pending` is `pub` and any future caller (or refactor that moves it inside an async context, a #[tauri::command], or another spawn) will silently deadlock on the runtime thread. Either gate the call site explicitly (`#[track_caller]` + runtime assertion), split the async DB into sync variants for recovery, or restructure so the recovery runs inside a dedicated runtime.

The last assertion references `&rf` but this function defines the variable as `bad`, not `rf`. There is no `rf` in scope here — `rf` is defined only in unrelated tests (e.g., `validate_rules_accepts_delete_without_archive_dir`). This is a hard compile error: no test in `migration::tests` can run until this is fixed. Replace `&rf` with `&bad`.

The victim DELETE runs in a separate statement before the INSERT, so an INSERT error irreversibly loses the evicted row; also removing only one row per insert never converges when the table already exceeds a lowered capacity (e.g. after tuning capacity is reduced). Wrap the count/victim selection, DELETE, and INSERT in a single transaction and trim down to capacity when needed.

Writers accept embeddings of any dimension, with NaN/Inf components, and zero vectors without validation, even though blob_to_embedding rejects malformed blobs on read. Such vectors are persisted and later returned by load_all, silently breaking semantic dedup (cosine returns None) and retrieval while the insert call reports success. Validate length == EMBED_DIM, finiteness, and non‑zero norm at the shared write boundary.

content: JournalEntry cannot round-trip through the on-disk journal it is supposed to enable. The doc comment above explicitly states this table is replayed at startup to repair the DB after a crash, but the struct only derives `Debug, Clone` — no `Serialize`/`Deserialize`. Without these derives the journal rows cannot be persisted by `serde_json`/`bincode`/`rmp_serde` (whichever the migration layer uses), so the very lost-update/孤儿-file scenario this struct exists to prevent is the one that cannot be recovered. Add `Serialize, Deserialize` (and a `#[serde(rename_all = ...)]` if a stable on-disk schema matters).

This makes invalid states representable and forces every consumer (replay, apply, reporting) to re-parse and re-validate the same string. Model them as `enum JournalOp { Move, Delete }` and `enum RuleAction { Move, Delete }` (with `#[serde(rename_all = "lowercase")]`) so an unknown variant fails fast at the (de)serialize boundary and the rest of the code can exhaustively `match` without `unwrap`/default branches.

content: TOCTOU between resolve and create/verify: resolve_archive_dir_checked only canonicalizes the deepest *existing* ancestor; the residual window between this return and the subsequent create_dir_all (or verify_archive_dir_created) allows a concurrent symlink swap to redirect the archive outside the desktop base. The inline comment defers this to a Phase-6 follow-up, but in the meantime any caller that creates the resolved dir before the verify is exposed to a real path-escape. Consider performing create_dir_all *before* the verify (and re-checking), or hard-link the verify back into resolve so the caller cannot act on a stale result.

claim_dst_name → move_entry TOCTOU with cross-platform overwrite risk: claim_dst_name picks a non-existing name, but the actual fs::rename/fs::copy inside move_entry can race another worker that wins the same slot; fs::copy silently overwrites on Unix when the dst was created in the window, so the documented 99-iteration protection does not prevent data loss — only prevents a livelock. Either open dst with O_EXCL|O_CREAT (Unix) and treat AlreadyExists as retry, or place each move under a staging sibling like copy_dir_recursive does, so the final commit is an atomic rename.

The derived `Deserialize` only accepts the exact lowercase variants, but the doc comment at the top describes a `Widget/未标记` fallback — i.e. missing or unrecognized source values should be classified as `Widget`. With this derive, any incoming event whose `source` is absent or contains an unknown string will fail to deserialize into `MutationOrigin`, so the documented fallback must be implemented at the call site (e.g. `Option<MutationOrigin>` with a custom mapping). That contract is not enforced by the type system; consider `#[serde(other)]` on `Widget`, or a separate wrapper enum, to make the fallback explicit and impossible to forget.

Prefer making `run_migration_inner` `async` (and letting callers `.await` it) or move all DB I/O onto a dedicated blocking thread that owns its own runtime, instead of relying on a fragile "never call me from a tokio thread" contract.

content: `journal_cleared` and `journal_committed` are the only thing closing the loop between filesystem state and DB state — discarding their errors with `.ok()` means a wedged journal row is silently ignored. On the next start, `journal_replay_pending` will re-attempt the move/delete: if the original move actually succeeded, replay will see src gone + dst present and re-issue the DB fix (wasted work); if the original move/delete failed and `journal_cleared` was the cleanup that didn't happen, every subsequent run repeats the same failing operation and can stack up duplicate copies in the archive dir. Log the failure (and/or surface a counter on `report`) so an operator can see "5 journal commits failed this run" instead of a forever-spinning recovery.

Either block UNC/`file:` explicitly (e.g., also reject `\\` prefixes and `file:`/`ftp:`/etc. schemes) or document that UNC is in scope and gate it via the permission prompt path.

content: The three failure branches after `SetClipboardData(CF_HDROP, ...)` has committed (title `GlobalAlloc` failure, title `GlobalLock` null, title `SetClipboardData` failure) each independently have to remember to (a) `GlobalFree` the title handle on the title-handle paths, (b) `EmptyClipboard` so the clipboard does not silently retain a stale file, and (c) `CloseClipboard` so subsequent `OpenClipboard` calls do not stall. Today all three paths do this correctly, but the invariants are spread across three near-identical match arms with no shared helper — one missed `EmptyClipboard` would re-introduce the "user sees 'copy failed' yet paste still delivers the file" bug that the surrounding `//  #4` and `//  #119` comments specifically call out as historical regressions. Extracting a small `fn finalize_post_hdrop(th: Option<HGLOBAL>)` would localize the invariant and make regressions much harder.

Cross-key semantic merge overwrites `content` and the full `tags` list, destroying the original key reference (only surfaced via `orig_key`). A semantically-similar write with a different key can silently replace a distinct fact without any source/trust guard. Consider adding a same-key requirement (or stricter source/kind checks) before merge, or at minimum asserting that the target's key can still be looked up after merge.

Near-threshold refusal test only asserts `len == 1` and the outcome variant. It does NOT verify the target row's `content`/`tags` are unchanged. If the implementation performed the merge UPDATE before refusing, the row count stays 1 but the target is silently corrupted and the test would still pass. Add `content` and `tags` assertions on the surviving row.

FAIL-OPEN after deserialization: load_rules_from returns the deserialized RulesFile without calling validate_rules, so a persisted rule with action == "move" and an empty archiveDir passes load but `resolve_archive_dir` at runtime resolves the empty string to the desktop base directory — destructive files move to the wrong place. Additionally, RulesFile.version is read from the file but never compared against the supported version (currently 1); a future format with incompatible semantics would be silently accepted and acted on. Call validate_rules(&r)? after deserialization (mapping the validation error to CommandError::DomainRule) and reject unsupported versions before returning.

Concurrent save race: there is no locking around the load → mutate → save cycle, and db::atomic_write writes to a fixed sibling tmp path (`<name>.tmp`). Two concurrent save_rules calls can interleave so that one writer's rename succeeds with the other writer's bytes (false Ok response) while the loser fails because its tmp is gone (false Err); user-authored rules can be silently overwritten. Wrap the RMW pair in a process-level mutex or OS file lock so that the read–modify–write cycle is serialized; pairing this with the load-side fix in load_rules_from closes the integrity gap end-to-end.

`OpenOptions::create(true).append(true)` on Unix does NOT set 0600 — the new file is created with mode `0666 & ~umask` (typically 0644), directly contradicting the comment "创建即 0600（与 audit::open_log_append 一致）" and `audit::open_log_append` (which explicitly chmods the freshly-created file to 0o600, per src-tauri/src/audit.rs:343). Concrete impact: the fallback `bot.log` here ends up world-readable while audit-created `bot.log` is owner-only; if both writers ever race (this file is opened without `BOT_LOG_LOCK` from a detached thread, while audit opens under the lock), the file ends up owned by this function's process but readable by all users, leaking `exe_dir`/`resolved` path info. Either set the mode explicitly (`OpenOptions::new().create(true).append(true).mode(0o600)` on Unix, or call `set_permissions(0o600)` after open — matching audit's pattern), or drop the comment claim. Also consider whether existing pre-existing files should be chmod'd on each write (audit does this on first open); at minimum, also chmod if `metadata().mode() != 0o600` so existing files from older, non-0600-aware runs get tightened.

Storing src/dst via `Path::to_string_lossy()` collapses any non‑UTF‑8 byte sequence to U+FFFD, so two distinct filesystem paths that only differ by invalid UTF‑8 bytes map to the same SQLite TEXT value. The journal is later queried by (task_id, src) during replay, so colliding entries will silently overwrite each other and recovery may operate on the wrong file. Validate that paths are valid UTF‑8 before writing, or store a lossless representation (e.g. escaped OsString) and reject non‑UTF‑8 paths outright.

The INSERT into migration_journal reuses `src.to_string_lossy()` for the src column; the same lossy conversion issue applies here. Combined with the SELECT above, a non‑UTF‑8 src path is silently mangled both when written and when read, masking duplicate entries. Use the validated UTF‑8 string from above (`src_s`) instead of calling `to_string_lossy()` again.

`journal_committed_inner` updates the state without checking that the row is currently `pending`, so a stale id (or a row that was already cleared) is silently flipped to `committed`. This breaks the pending→committed/cleared state machine and can resurrect rows whose underlying file operation never happened, causing replay to act on a ghost entry. Add the `state = 'pending'` predicate and verify rows_affected so callers see a hard error on stale ids.

`journal_cleared_inner` has the same state‑machine gap as `journal_committed_inner`: the UPDATE accepts any id and silently flips a row that may already be `committed` (or another non‑pending state) back to `cleared`, destroying evidence of a completed operation. Restrict the transition to pending and surface a typed error when no row was updated.

content: Mutex poison is swallowed and the lock is salvaged via `e.into_inner()`, then execution continues as if nothing happened. If a previous thread panicked mid-write, the log file can be in an inconsistent state (partial line, missing flush, half-rotated file) yet subsequent audit entries will be appended on top of that corruption. For an audit/security log this is a data-integrity hazard — at minimum, log the poisoning to the audit log itself (or to a fallback sink) before recovering, and consider failing the write so the caller knows the audit line was not durably recorded.

Both filesystem failures are silently dropped: `if let Ok(mut f) = open_log_append(path)` discards the open error, and `let _ = writeln!(f, "[{ts}] {safe}")` discards the write/flush error. For a security/audit trail this is a real data-loss bug — an audit line that fails to open or fails to flush vanishes with no signal to the caller and no fallback record. Surface the error (at least propagate a `Result`, or write a fallback entry to a secondary sink / `eprintln!` with structured context) instead of unconditionally returning `()`.

notif_sync_memory rewrites the JSON payload with only `{"ids": remaining}`, discarding every other key that may have been stored. If the payload ever carries additional metadata (e.g. session id, timestamps, summaries), this UPDATE will silently delete that information. Preserve the original payload by merging `remaining` into the existing object instead of replacing it.

`notif_resolve_artifact` loads every pending artifact notification, parses each payload in Rust, and only then filters by `taskId`. With many pending rows this is O(N) memory + JSON parsing per call. Use SQLite's `json_extract` (or a dedicated indexed column) so the filter runs in SQL, and wrap the updates in a transaction so a failure leaves the table consistent.

`notif_sync_memory` issues one `SELECT COUNT(*)` per id (N+1 queries) and `unwrap_or(false)` swallows any DB error as "not present". If a transient error occurs or the payload contains non‑integer ids, `remaining` can become empty and the notification will be prematurely resolved. Fetch the pending ids in a single query, build a `HashSet`, and treat unknown/parse‑error IDs as fatal for that notification rather than silently discarding them.

Per-call working directory is created under `py_runs_root` and never removed. Every successful or failed invocation of `run_dotnet_revisions` permanently leaks a UUID-named directory (plus `params.json`), so disk usage grows unboundedly for any user who triggers the .NET revisions path more than once. Use `tempfile::TempDir` (auto-cleans on drop), or explicitly `std::fs::remove_dir_all(&dir)` in both the success and error arms before returning, so cleanup happens even when `run_python_at` returns `Err`.

`drain_output` uses stringly-typed dispatch (`if kind == "out"`) and returns a 4-tuple `(String, String, bool, bool)` of anonymous values. A typo or new variant on the producer side silently misroutes stdout into stderr, and the call sites must remember which bool is "got==2" vs "truncated". Replace the `&'static str` channel tag with a shared enum (e.g. `enum Stream { Stdout, Stderr }`) and return a small named struct so the contract is self-evident and type-checked.

`read_capped_drain` swallows the read error: when `read_to_end` fails mid-stream, `buf` is returned with `truncated == false`, so callers cannot distinguish a complete-but-truncated read from an interrupted read that left output incomplete (the comment explicitly warns about "假完整" output). Surface the failure — e.g. return `(Vec<u8>, TruncationStatus)` with a `Complete | Truncated | Interrupted` enum, or return `io::Result<(Vec<u8>, bool)>` — so the caller is forced to handle it instead of silently shipping partial output to the user.

`join_reader_threads` silently detaches the reader thread on timeout: after logging the leak it drops the `JoinHandle` via the `for` loop iteration end, leaving the OS thread running. Because the reader typically owns the `Sender` end of an `mpsc::channel` (and the child's stdout/stderr pipes), a still-running reader will block forever on its next `send` once the receiver is dropped, and the child's pipe FDs / handles stay live in the kernel — producing exactly the kind of "reader_leaked" accumulation this function tries to surface. Either close the receiver-side explicitly before/after the timeout (so the sender errors out and the reader exits), or have the reader thread observe a shared shutdown signal so it actually terminates.

TOCTOU between the symlink check and the subsequent `rename`/`copy_rec`: `symlink_metadata(&src)` is consulted, then later `std::fs::rename(&src, &dest)` (or `copy_rec`) acts on the same path with no atomic guarantee. A concurrent writer can swap a regular file for a symlink inside that window — and the very comment above the check explicitly acknowledges that `rename` would then move the symlink itself into `AI_Gen_Files` while its target stays outside `dir`, defeating the defence. Resolve once and operate on the same handle (e.g. `DirEntry` + `renameat`/`renameat2` with `RENAME_NOREPLACE`, or open with `O_NOFOLLOW` and use `renameat` on the fd) instead of re-stat'ing the path.

`copy_rec` aborts via `?` on the first failing child, but the just-created `dest` directory plus any successfully-copied siblings stay on disk. That contradicts the harvest-rollback path's whole rationale of "no orphan copies". Track whether `create_dir_all(dest)` ran and, on any recursion error, `remove_dir_all(dest)` before propagating the error so callers see a clean all-or-nothing copy.

`sweep_stale_py_runs_in` reports a misleading count: `removed += 1` runs whether or not `std::fs::remove_dir_all(&p)` actually succeeded (the error is discarded by `let _`). Permission errors, locked files on Windows, or transient I/O issues are silently counted as successes and never reach `py_audit`. Increment only on `Ok`, and surface failures — either a second counter for `failed` or per-entry audit lines — so operators can see when stale dirs can't be reaped.

Excel formula-injection guard is incomplete: the comment itself names the threat (WEBSERVICE/DDE on open), but the runtime check only catches cells whose openpyxl data_type is `'f'`. (1) When the model emits values like `'+1+1'`, `'-2+3'`, `'@SUM(...)'` Excel/Calc still evaluate them on open, and openpyxl may persist them as string `'s'` (or worse, as `'f'`) depending on value origin. (2) The guard inspects only the last appended row (`ws[ws.max_row]`); cells added via direct assignment, merges, or later `ws.append` calls later in the iteration are not re-scanned. Recommend sanitizing any string cell value whose first char is in `=+-@` (or its trimmed form starts with one) at write time, and applying the guard to every cell of the appended row (e.g. iterate `ws[ws.max_row]` after each append AND a final sweep over all populated cells).

`file_path_to_string` returns the raw URL for the `Url` variant (e.g. `file:///home/u/a.docx`). That string is then handed to `EXTRACT_SCRIPT` and `MAKE_DOCX_REVISIONS_SCRIPT`, both of which call `os.path.exists(p)` / `docx.Document(p)` / `shutil.copyfile(path, out)`. On POSIX `os.path.exists("file:///...")` is always False, so the script falls through to the "缺少原文" error path even when the user selected a real file via a system dialog that returns the URL form. Convert to a filesystem path (e.g. `url.to_file_path()` / strip the `file://` scheme) before returning, or only return `Some` for the `Path` variant.

`profile_remove_avatar` deletes whatever path `profile_dir(&app).join(f)` resolves to without re‑validating `f` via `avatar_filename_only`. A hand‑edited / imported / corrupt `profile.json` can put values such as `"../../wmessage.db"`, `"/etc/passwd"`, `"a\\b.png"` or even an absolute path into `avatar`; after the function successfully clears the JSON reference (which only requires the read‑modify‑write lock) the next line will unlink that arbitrary file with the privileges of the Tauri process. Because the field is also accepted from the IPC layer, this is reachable from any compromised renderer as well. Validate the stored name through `avatar_filename_only` (rejecting `None`) and, on rejection, audit the event instead of deleting. Optionally also verify the resolved path is a child of `profile_dir` (canonicalize both) before `remove_file`.

`profile_set_avatar` deletes *all* prior avatars for this `kind` **before** the new avatar is committed. If `std::fs::copy`, `save_data`, or the final `rename` later fails, `profile.json` is left pointing at the old filename (or at the new filename when the save succeeded but the rename did not) while the old file is already gone — the user's previous avatar is silently lost with no rollback path. Defer deletion of the previously stored avatar (and any other‑extension siblings) until **after** `rename(&dest_tmp, &dest)` succeeds; only then look up the prior `entry.avatar` recorded before the overwrite and remove it. The cleanup loop should keep `dest` (or the old extension's file) untouched until the new file is on disk.

The new avatar is committed in the order `save_data(&profile.json)` → `rename(&dest_tmp, &dest)`. Because `profile.json` is updated *before* the on‑disk file is in place, a failure of `rename` (cross‑device move, AV/EBUSY, Windows sharing violation, quota, etc.) leaves `profile.json` pointing at a filename that does not exist (or, after the old file was removed by the earlier cleanup loop, pointing at a file that was never created). The function then returns `Err`, but the persisted state is already inconsistent — the next `profile_get` will return `avatar_data_url=None`. Reverse the ordering: perform `rename(&dest_tmp, &dest)` first while the old entry is still in the JSON, then call `save_data`. If `save_data` fails after the rename, `cleanup_set_avatar_failure` can be extended to revert the rename using `rename(&dest, &dest_tmp)` (or, on platforms where rename‑over‑existing isn’t atomic, remove the new file).

`ensure_person_id` has a classic RMW race: both `pid` (generated before the lock) and `data.person_id` (read inside the lock) are used independently. When two first‑run callers race, each persists *its own* `pid` to `profile.json` via the double‑check (only the second sees the first's write, the first has already finished), and then both still call `people_upsert_entry(&pid, …, is_self=true)` using their *local* `pid`. Result: two self rows in `people` with different ids while only one of them ends up in `profile.json`; every subsequent export uses the surviving id and the orphan self row leaks. On `save_data` failure the function still upserts `pid` and returns it as if persisted, breaking the documented "固化 idempotent" contract and producing a fresh self row on the next call. Fix: under the lock load `profile.json`, compute the canonical pid (`existing or newly generated`), write it, capture it from the locked `data`, and use that canonical value for the `people_upsert_entry` and the return tuple; also propagate the `save_data` error (change the signature to `CommandResult`) so the caller does not get a non‑persistent pid.

`entry_view` blindly `metadata()`/`read()`s whatever file sits at `profile_dir(app).join(f)`. The filename validation only rejects literal `/`, `\` and `..`; it does **not** inspect the file itself. If an attacker (or a hostile dropper in a portable install on a shared drive) can plant a symlink at `profile/avatar-user.png` pointing at e.g. `~/.ssh/id_rsa`, the next `profile_get` will read that file, base64‑encode it, and emit it to every window via the `profile-changed` IPC event. Use `std::fs::symlink_metadata` and reject (audit + `None`) when the entry's `file_type().is_symlink()` is true, or open with `OpenOptions::new().read(true).custom_flags(libc::O_NOFOLLOW)` on platforms that support it.

Prompt instructs `run_python` for bulk cross-file edits and data processing, but the underlying tool (`SCHEMA_RUN_PYTHON`, `run_python_ungated` in `py/runtime.rs`) explicitly provides "无文件系统隔离" — only CPU/memory/time limits are enforced, no chroot/path restriction, so arbitrary Python can read/write anywhere on the user's filesystem, spawn subprocesses, and access the network. The "安全红线" at the end ("绝不执行系统命令、修改系统设置、访问系统目录"; write-tool whitelist "白名单外弹确认") is purely prompt-level and is actively defeated by rule 12 ("用户要写代码/跑数据处理时用 run_python") and rule 19 ("同一处改动散布多个文件或多处重复出现时，用 run_python 批量替换比逐个 edit_file 更高效可靠"). Either tighten the prompt to forbid run_python from touching whitelisted paths / launching subprocesses (relying on prompt adherence is fragile), or back the tool with a real sandbox (chroot, macOS sandbox-exec, Windows Job Object + restricted token, container) so the security red lines become enforced invariants instead of advisory text.

content: VECTOR_CACHE is held across the synchronous `embed_text` call, so a single slow ONNX inference serializes every concurrent caller — including pure cache hits from unrelated commands — for the full inference latency. The inline comment justifies the trade-off, but `tag_similar_pairs` is not the only path that touches this global; any future reader/writer of `VECTOR_CACHE` will block. Drop the lock before the blocking call and re-acquire it just for the insert; the brief race window on a cache miss is acceptable for this workload and can be tightened later with a single-flight guard (e.g. `DashMap` entry API) if duplicate ONNX calls actually show up in profiling.

Guard's ownership check is only `subagent_id` equality, so an ABA scenario — same `session_id` + same `subagent_id` reused by a retry/resume — causes the old guard's Drop to delete the newer runner's registration. This silently disables the recursion gate (`is_subagent_session` returns false) for the live subagent, allowing it to spawn further subagents. The ownership identity should be unique (e.g. an `Arc<()>` weak token, generation counter, or guard-issued nonce) not just a string field that is expected to repeat.

`register_subagent_session` blindly overwrites an existing entry, replacing the `Arc<AtomicUsize>` budget counter. A duplicate registration (retry/reuse of the same session_id, or a buggy double-spawn) resets `used_tool_calls` to whatever the new caller supplies — a second runner can effectively nullify `max_tool_calls` enforcement. Callers that already hold a clone of the old context can still increment the *detached* old counter, bypassing any future re-check. Either reject duplicate keys, or require the new context to carry the *same* `Arc<AtomicUsize>` (carry-and-check) so the counter is preserved across retries.

The task-execution-flow registry has no RAII guard, no ownership check, and no idempotency token. A panic between `register_exec_session` and `unregister_exec_session` permanently leaks the entry (making `is_task_execution_flow` always true). Conversely, session-ID reuse causes the new registration to be silently overwritten, and a late `unregister_exec_session` from the previous (stale) runner removes the new entry — misclassifying a live task execution as a plain conversation. Both `register_exec_session` and `unregister_exec_session` should be wrapped in a guard analogous to `SubagentSessionGuard`, or at minimum check that the current entry's origin matches the one the caller originally registered.

`validate_attach_path` (lines 409-428) canonicalizes the user-supplied path and inspects only the resolved extension — it does not verify that the canonical path lives under any allow-listed directory (e.g. user's home, app data dir, or a project root). The accompanying comment claims "用户在对话框亲手选的文件 = 明确授权", so the design trusts the caller; this assumption is fine for the chat-dialog picker, but the function is `fn` (no `pub`/`pub(crate)`) and is only invoked from `build_attachment_blocks`, whose input comes straight from the `attachments: Option<Vec<String>>` invoke parameter — which an attacker (or a malicious frontend module) can fabricate. The current behavior will happily open any readable .docx/.xlsx/.pptx/.pdf on the host (e.g. `/etc/shadow.docx`, `~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pdf`, browser cookies exports). At minimum, add a directory-containment check (e.g. `canon.starts_with(allowed_root)`) or take the allowed-root list as an argument from the trusted caller.

Re-including `tests/mock_llm.rs` via `include!` re-registers every `#[tokio::test]` defined there inside the bot_test_connection binary, so mock_llm's own tests will run twice across the suite (and any shared mutable state across runs could interact). Prefer placing the shared mock under `tests/common/` (a non-test module) and importing from both test binaries, or guard the duplicated tests with `#[cfg(...)]` so they only register in one binary.

Latent bug in `py_gate_acquire_inner`: the second EXITING branch (`*avail += 1`) increments the permit count without a preceding decrement. The comment claims "归还许可" (return permit) but no permit was taken, so if this branch were ever reached under different locking semantics it would leak a phantom permit and let an extra task past the gate. Currently unreachable because both EXITING checks run under the same `PY_PERMITS` mutex guard (the atomic value cannot change between them), but the code does not match its documented intent and is a maintenance hazard.

Empty LLM result is not idempotent. The pre-read guard only skips when `tags` is already Some(non-empty), and an empty parse result is returned as Ok(Some(vec![])) without persisting any attempt marker. Subsequent invocations that find `tags` still empty will re-enter the full LLM path, contradicting the module-level claim that the guard chain is idempotent. Consider persisting an explicit "attempted, no tags" state (e.g. a separate column or a sentinel tag) or returning a distinct Ok(None) variant so repeated fire-and-forget calls do not re-invoke the model.</content>

Retry loop only retries JSON validation failures; provider/network errors break immediately, contradicting the module doc "失败重试 1 次" and the function comment "失败重试 1 次，再失败降级空 questions". A single transient API/5xx error therefore permanently skips clarification instead of honouring the promised one retry.

Only the attachment *count* is bounded (≤10); each path string is forwarded as-is to `build_attachment_blocks` and then into the prompt / error messages. A renderer/XSS can ship a multi-MB single path that (a) bloats memory and (b) gets injected verbatim into the model prompt and audit error text, providing a free exfiltration / cost-amplification vector. Reject paths that exceed a sane limit (e.g. OS PATH_MAX, 4 KiB) before any further processing.
